meta.blurb: Blow out a candle and hold a flame to the rising vapour, and the fire jumps down and relights the wick. Michael Faraday did this for children, then used one candle to explain water, air and even your own breathing.
meta.bible: Michael Faraday: English scientist, born in 1791 in London, the son of a blacksmith. He left school young, was apprenticed to a bookbinder, read the books he bound, and became assistant to Humphry Davy. The Royal Institution: a scientific society in London where Faraday worked. He gave its Christmas Lectures for young people; he gave his series on The Chemical History of a Candle at Christmas 1848, and again in 1860 and 1861. The book: six lectures, printed in 1861 from notes taken by William Crookes. Lecture titles in order: A Candle, Brightness of Flame, Products of Combustion, Hydrogen in the Candle, Oxygen and the Air, Carbon and Breathing. The experiments: a Candle, Wick, Tallow, Beeswax, Spermaceti, Capillary attraction, Vapour, Davy's safety lamp and Wire gauze, the Argand burner and Chimney, Soot, Camphor, Turpentine, Ice and salt freezing mixture, Potassium, Battery and Electricity, Hydrogen, Oxygen, Chlorate of potash, Manganese, Nitrogen, Atmosphere, Pressure, Limewater, Carbonic acid (the old name of carbon dioxide, which this book calls Carbon dioxide), Charcoal, Carbon, Coal gas, Respiration, Combustion, Compound, Particles. Everything in this book is a real demonstration of Faraday's or a plain fact of chemistry; no number is invented. Voice: warm, clear and curious, like Faraday speaking to children; one small flame leads to the biggest ideas. Fixed facts added for the full-length book (all real): Faraday was born on 22 September 1791 at Newington Butts, south of London; his father James was a blacksmith; at 14 he was apprenticed to the bookbinder George Riebau for seven years; he read the Encyclopaedia Britannica and Jane Marcet's Conversations on Chemistry; in 1812 a customer, William Dance, gave him tickets to hear Humphry Davy; in 1813 he became Davy's assistant and toured Europe with Davy until 1815, meeting Volta and Ampere; in 1825 he began the Christmas Lectures; in 1831 he found electromagnetic induction; he died on 25 August 1867 at Hampton Court aged 75. Davy and Faraday burned a diamond in Florence in 1814. Other names: Jan Ingenhousz (Dutch doctor who showed in 1779 that plants need sunlight), Robert Bunsen (German chemist, Bunsen burner of the 1850s), William Crookes (took the notes of the 1860 lectures, printed 1861), Aime Argand, Alessandro Volta, Michel Chevreul, Joseph Priestley, Antoine Lavoisier, Jacques Charles, Paris, Britain, Japan, Highgate. Technical words, kept as names so the book may use them: Lycopodium, Platinum, Iron, Zinc, Sulphur, Phosphorus, Sulphuric, Saltpetre, Gunpowder, Lime, Quicklime, Chalk, Marble, Limestone, Calcium, Methane, Firedamp, Filings, Steam, Cotton, Plaited, Snuffers, Rushlight, Stearin, Paraffin, Taper, Beaker, Flask, Trough, Burner, Lamp, Lampblack, Graphite, Diamond, Coke, Tar, Gasworks, Lungs, Blood, Sugar, Starch, Celsius, Faraday, Induction, Magnet, Magnetic, Dynamo, Generator, Motor, Farad, Crookes, Bladder, Retort, Lens, Fuel, Soda, Dioxide, Celsius, Litre, Kilogram, Centimetre. Carbon dioxide is written as two words and is a plain gas. The six lectures are told in order: chapters 16-17 end with carbon dioxide, charcoal and coal gas, 18 is breathing, 19 plants and the carbon circle (Priestley's mint in 1771), 20 the farewell. Chapters 1-6 are the first lecture and Faraday's life, chapters 7-9 the second, 10-11 the third, 12 the fourth, 13-15 the fifth, 16-20 the sixth and the farewell.

beats.scene: A lecture hall full of children watching a man light a candle
beats.summary: Lecture 1: at the Royal Institution in London, Michael Faraday lights one candle in front of a young audience.

beats.scene: Families climbing a grand staircase on a winter evening toward a lecture hall
beats.summary: Every Christmas the Royal Institution holds lectures for young people, and Faraday loves to give them.

beats.scene: A long table crowded with glass jars, tubes, a trough and a small burner
beats.summary: Faraday's table holds only simple apparatus that the audience can see clearly.

beats.scene: Faraday stands behind the candle and begins to speak to the hall
beats.summary: He names his subject, the chemical history of a candle, and admits that it sounds like a small thing.

beats.scene: A candle with three big question marks chalked on a blackboard behind it
beats.summary: He promises to answer three questions: how the wax reaches the flame, why the flame shines, and where the candle goes.

beats.scene: Six numbered lecture cards pinned in a row above the table
beats.summary: The talks will run to six lectures, from the flame itself to the breath of the audience.

beats.scene: Children leaning forward on benches with their hands raised
beats.summary: Faraday asks his young listeners to watch closely and to ask questions about everything they see.

beats.scene: A Victorian parlour lit by a candle and an oil lamp
beats.summary: In 1848 most homes were lit by candles and oil lamps, and gas lit the streets of big cities.

beats.scene: A close view of a candle flame showing yellow, blue and a dark centre
beats.summary: Looking closely, the flame is not one colour: it is yellow at the top, blue below and dark in the middle.

beats.scene: An adult kneeling beside a child who holds a lit candle over a plate
beats.summary: Fire is useful but dangerous, and these experiments should be tried only with an adult beside you.

beats.scene: A blacksmith at a glowing forge in a village south of London
beats.summary: Michael Faraday was born on 22 September 1791 near London, the son of a blacksmith.

beats.scene: A thin boy holding a single loaf of bread outside a bakery
beats.summary: His family was poor, and he went to school only long enough to learn to read, write and count.

beats.scene: A boy in a cap delivers newspapers along a London street
beats.summary: At thirteen he began work as an errand boy for the bookseller George Riebau.

beats.scene: An apprentice sews pages and glues leather at a bookbinder's bench
beats.summary: At fourteen he was apprenticed to Riebau for seven years to learn the trade of bookbinding.

beats.scene: A boy reads a thick book by candlelight on a workshop bench
beats.summary: He read the books he bound, especially an article on electricity and Jane Marcet's book on chemistry.

beats.scene: A boy builds a small electrical machine from a glass bottle
beats.summary: He tried the experiments for himself, using a glass bottle and a few simple parts.

beats.scene: A shopkeeper hands two paper tickets to a young apprentice
beats.summary: In 1812 a customer, William Dance, gave him tickets to hear the chemist Humphry Davy lecture.

beats.scene: A young man binds his own pages of lecture notes into a book
beats.summary: He copied out his notes into a book of about three hundred pages and sent it to Davy.

beats.scene: A famous scientist shows a young assistant a glass jar in a laboratory
beats.summary: In 1813 Davy hired him as an assistant, and they toured Europe together.

beats.scene: Faraday at a lectern before a crowd of children in a hall
beats.summary: Faraday became a great scientist, and in 1825 he began the Christmas Lectures.

beats.scene: Candles of yellow tallow, pale wax and white fat in a row
beats.summary: Faraday shows candles made of different materials, to show that a candle can be made from many fuels.

beats.scene: A butcher's cart of animal fat beside a pot of melting tallow
beats.summary: Tallow, the fat of cattle and sheep, made the cheapest candles of all.

beats.scene: Honeybees at work on a honeycomb with a block of pale wax
beats.summary: Beeswax comes from honeybees and makes clean, sweet-smelling candles.

beats.scene: A pale waxy candle beside a drawing of a sperm whale
beats.summary: Spermaceti, a wax from the sperm whale, made fine, hard and expensive candles.

beats.scene: A French chemist in a laboratory holds up a white candle
beats.summary: In the 1820s the chemist Michel Chevreul helped to find how to make stearin candles from fat.

beats.scene: A tallow maker dips rows of wicks into a pot of hot fat
beats.summary: Many candles were made by dipping a wick again and again into melted fat.

beats.scene: A rush stem held in an iron clip burns with a weak small flame
beats.summary: Poor families burned rushlights, which were dry rushes dipped in fat.

beats.scene: A hand with brass snuffers trims the long black tip of a wick
beats.summary: A candle's wick is twisted cotton, and old wicks often bent over and smoked until they were trimmed.

beats.scene: A plaited wick curls over to the edge of a bright flame
beats.summary: A plaited wick curls to the edge of the flame, where it burns away and needs no trimming.

beats.scene: A candle marked with lines beside a window at night
beats.summary: Before clocks were common, people marked lines on candles to tell the time.

beats.scene: A match touches a candle wick and a tiny blue flame appears
beats.summary: When the candle is lit the flame is small and blue at first, and then it grows.

beats.scene: A candle with a small clear pool of melted wax around its flame
beats.summary: The heat melts the wax around the wick and makes a little cup of liquid.

beats.scene: A close view of a hard white rim around a pool of wax
beats.summary: The rim of the cup stays solid because the air rushing past it keeps it cool.

beats.scene: A candle in a draught with wax running down one side of it
beats.summary: In a draught the cooling is uneven, so the rim melts and the wax runs down one side.

beats.scene: A candle drawn as a lamp, with a labelled bowl of liquid fuel
beats.summary: A candle is a lamp that makes its own bowl and holds its own liquid fuel.

beats.scene: Wax climbs up a wick in a close picture, drawn with little arrows
beats.summary: The liquid wax climbs the wick through the tiny spaces between its threads.

beats.scene: A sponge and a towel dipping into water, with the water climbing up
beats.summary: A sponge or the corner of a towel also draws water up above the level of the pool.

beats.scene: Water standing at different heights in thin and wide glass tubes
beats.summary: Water climbs higher in a thinner tube, which is why this action is called capillary attraction.

beats.scene: A sugar cube dipped at its corner into a cup of tea
beats.summary: A sugar cube touching tea soon becomes wet all the way up.

beats.scene: A burning candle with a thin and a thick wick side by side
beats.summary: Only the tip of the wick burns, and a wick that is too thick brings up too much fuel.

beats.scene: A blown-out candle with a white trail of smoke rising from the wick
beats.summary: When the candle is blown out, a thin white trail of vapour rises from the wick.

beats.scene: A lighted taper in the smoke, with a flame leaping down to the wick
beats.summary: A flame brought near the trail jumps down it and relights the candle.

beats.scene: A drawing of solid wax, liquid wax and rising vapour in three steps
beats.summary: The fuel makes a journey: solid wax melts, the liquid turns to vapour, and the vapour burns.

beats.scene: A thin glass tube with one end in the dark middle of a flame
beats.summary: Faraday pushes one end of a glass tube into the dark middle of the flame to collect its vapour.

beats.scene: A bent glass tube carries vapour from a flame to a second flame
beats.summary: The vapour comes out of the far end of the tube and burns there as a second flame.

beats.scene: A square of card pressed flat on a flame, scorched in a ring
beats.summary: A card pressed on the flame turns brown in a ring, so the burning is at the outside.

beats.scene: A fine wire gauze held over a candle flame that stops it rising
beats.summary: A fine wire gauze held over the flame will not let the fire pass through it.

beats.scene: A gauze over a candle with a second small flame burning above it
beats.summary: Smoke lit above the gauze burns there, but the fire does not travel down.

beats.scene: A miner with a small lamp in a dark coal mine tunnel
beats.summary: Humphry Davy used the gauze to make a safe lamp for coal miners in 1815.

beats.scene: A metal gauze cylinder around a lamp flame in a mine
beats.summary: The metal carries the heat away so quickly that the gas outside cannot catch fire.

beats.scene: A tall, pointed candle flame in still air, drawn like a tongue
beats.summary: In still air the flame is shaped like a tongue, tall and narrow with a pointed tip.

beats.scene: A candle with arrows showing hot air rising and cool air flowing in
beats.summary: The flame heats the air around it, which rises, while cooler air flows in from below.

beats.scene: A candle's shadow on a white screen with a dark ribbon rising above it
beats.summary: A bright lamp throws the shadow of the flame on a screen and shows the rising stream of hot air.

beats.scene: A candle flame leaning sideways as a child blows gently at it
beats.summary: A breath or a draught pushes the flame sideways and makes it flicker.

beats.scene: A Swiss inventor in a workshop holds a lamp with a round wick
beats.summary: In the 1780s Argand invented a lamp with a wick woven into a hollow ring.

beats.scene: A ring-shaped flame with arrows of air entering from outside and inside
beats.summary: Air reaches an Argand flame from outside and through its hollow middle, so it burns brightly.

beats.scene: A lamp with a tall glass chimney burning steadily in a dark room
beats.summary: A tall glass chimney draws a strong, steady stream of fresh air up to the flame.

beats.scene: A fireplace with a chimney carrying smoke up and out of a house
beats.summary: A chimney over a house fire works in just the same way.

beats.scene: A lighthouse at dusk with a bright lamp shining from its top
beats.summary: Argand lamps were bright enough to be used in lighthouses as well as in homes.

beats.scene: Faraday and a row of candles at the end of the first lecture
beats.summary: The first lecture ends with the main facts: the fuel melts, climbs, turns to vapour and burns.

beats.scene: Faraday at the table at the start of the second lecture
beats.summary: Lecture 2: Faraday recalls the first lecture and asks why a candle flame shines so brightly.

beats.scene: A pale blue spirit lamp flame beside a bright yellow candle flame
beats.summary: Some flames, such as a spirit lamp's, are pale and give almost no light.

beats.scene: Faraday points to a candle flame with a drawing of tiny specks beside it
beats.summary: Faraday suggests that a bright flame must hold tiny solid particles that glow.

beats.scene: A thin platinum wire glowing brightly in a pale flame
beats.summary: A thin platinum wire in a pale flame glows brightly, because a hot solid shines.

beats.scene: Iron filings falling through a flame in a shower of bright sparks
beats.summary: Iron filings sprinkled into a flame burn with bright sparks.

beats.scene: A puff of pale powder bursting into a great flash above a flame
beats.summary: Lycopodium powder blown through a flame burns at once in a great flash.

beats.scene: A blacksmith's iron glowing red, then orange, then white on an anvil
beats.summary: Any solid glows if it is hot enough, as the iron in a blacksmith's forge does.

beats.scene: A red-hot coal glowing in a fire without any flame
beats.summary: A glowing coal shines without a flame because it is a hot solid.

beats.scene: A drawing of vapour inside a flame breaking into black specks
beats.summary: Inside the flame the heat breaks the wax vapour apart and sets free tiny particles of carbon.

beats.scene: Tiny specks glowing in the flame and vanishing at its edge
beats.summary: The carbon particles glow white hot and burn away at the edge of the flame.

beats.scene: A cold white plate held in a flame and covered with black soot
beats.summary: A cold plate held in the flame is covered with black soot, which shows that the flame holds solid carbon.

beats.scene: A black powder in a dish beside a lump of charcoal and a diamond
beats.summary: The soot is carbon, the same substance as charcoal, and even the diamond is carbon.

beats.scene: A small block of white camphor burning with a thick black smoke
beats.summary: Camphor, a waxy solid from a tree, burns with a very smoky flame.

beats.scene: A cloth soaked in turpentine burns and sends up black clouds
beats.summary: Turpentine, made from pine sap, burns with thick black smoke.

beats.scene: A drawing of a smoky flame with too much carbon and too little air
beats.summary: These flames smoke because they hold more carbon than the air can burn at once.

beats.scene: A clean-burning candle flame with no smoke rising from it
beats.summary: A candle burns without smoke because it burns all its carbon.

beats.scene: An oil lamp with a high wick and a black plume of smoke
beats.summary: A lamp wick turned up too high makes the flame smoke.

beats.scene: Rows of chimneys over rooftops sending black smoke into a grey London sky
beats.summary: In Faraday's London, thousands of coal fires filled the air with smoke.

beats.scene: Black ink and a pot of paint beside a pile of soot
beats.summary: Fine soot, called lampblack, has long been used to make black ink and paint.

beats.scene: A candle burning in the dark with a question mark above its flame
beats.summary: Faraday asks where the carbon goes when a clean flame burns it all.

beats.scene: A candle burning under a glass jar, with the flame growing small and dim
beats.summary: A glass jar placed over a burning candle makes the flame grow dim, and then it goes out.

beats.scene: A glass jar full of air with a candle gone out inside it
beats.summary: The jar is still full of air, but the burning has changed it so that it cannot keep a flame alive.

beats.scene: Two candles in two bottles, one open and bright, one corked and low
beats.summary: A candle burns well in an open bottle but not in a closed one.

beats.scene: A candle on a wire being lowered into a tall glass jar
beats.summary: A candle lowered into a tall jar burns smaller and smaller as it goes down.

beats.scene: A blacksmith working a pair of bellows beside a glowing forge
beats.summary: A blacksmith makes a fire hotter by blowing air through it with bellows.

beats.scene: An Argand lamp with its middle air shut off, giving a dull smoky flame
beats.summary: If the air through the middle of an Argand burner is shut off, the flame goes dull and smokes.

beats.scene: A cast-iron stove with its door open and bright flames inside
beats.summary: A stove burns fast with its door and vents open, and slowly when they are shut.

beats.scene: A large jar and a small jar over two candles, one gone out sooner
beats.summary: A big jar lets a candle burn longer than a small one, because it holds more air.

beats.scene: A jar of air divided by a line, with one small part shaded
beats.summary: A candle uses up only one part of the air, and the rest does nothing to help it.

beats.scene: Faraday with a lit candle at the end of the second lecture
beats.summary: The second lecture ends with a promise that burning makes something new as well as using up air.

beats.scene: Faraday at the table with a lit candle and a row of cold glasses
beats.summary: Lecture 3: Faraday asks what a burning candle makes.

beats.scene: A cold glass beaker above a flame, covered with drops of water
beats.summary: A shiny, cold cup held over the flame is soon clouded with drops of water.

beats.scene: A metal vessel of ice and salt over a flame, dripping into a dish
beats.summary: A freezing mixture of ice and salt catches the water in larger quantities.

beats.scene: Clear drops running together into a small pool in a glass dish
beats.summary: The drops run together into a clear, colourless liquid that looks like water.

beats.scene: A warm cup stays dry above a flame while a cold one is wet
beats.summary: A warm cup stays dry, because the water stays in the air as invisible vapour.

beats.scene: A block of ice, a glass of water and a steaming kettle
beats.summary: Water is the same stuff as ice or steam, and Faraday shows all three of its forms.

beats.scene: A glass bottle split open by ice in a snowy garden
beats.summary: Water expands as it freezes, which can burst bottles and pipes.

beats.scene: A kettle with a clear gap between its spout and the white cloud
beats.summary: Steam itself is invisible, and the cloud above a kettle is made of tiny drops.

beats.scene: Rain over hills, a river running to the sea and clouds rising
beats.summary: Rain flows to the sea, the sun lifts water into the air again, and the cycle goes on.

beats.scene: A candle flame with a drop of water on a cold glass above it
beats.summary: Faraday says that a candle makes water as it burns, though he has yet to prove it.

beats.scene: A grey lump of potassium cut by a knife, beside a jar of oil
beats.summary: Faraday shows potassium, a soft silvery metal that is kept under oil.

beats.scene: A small piece of metal skating across water and bursting into a lilac flame
beats.summary: Dropped on water, potassium skates about and bursts into a lilac flame.

beats.scene: A little pool of water from a candle with a metal pellet in it
beats.summary: Dropped into the water from the candle, potassium burns in the same way, so the drops really are water.

beats.scene: Davy in his laboratory holding a tiny bright globule of metal
beats.summary: Humphry Davy first made potassium in 1807, using electricity.

beats.scene: A flame leaping above water with arrows showing gas escaping from it
beats.summary: The metal takes something from the water, and the gas that is set free is what burns.

beats.scene: A glowing iron tube with steam passing through it and a gas flame
beats.summary: Hot iron can also take something out of steam, and a gas that burns comes out.

beats.scene: A tall pile of metal discs and damp cloth beside a portrait of Volta
beats.summary: In 1800 Volta made the first battery, from discs of metal and damp cloth.

beats.scene: Two wires from a battery in a dish of water with bubbles rising
beats.summary: When wires from a battery are put in water, bubbles of gas rise from each wire.

beats.scene: Two glass tubes of gas standing in water, one filled twice as high
beats.summary: One tube fills with twice as much gas as the other, so water is made of two things.

beats.scene: Faraday writing notes by a battery in a laboratory
beats.summary: Faraday later studied electricity and chemistry closely and gave science words such as electrode and ion.

beats.scene: Faraday beside a row of glass jars at the start of lecture four
beats.summary: Lecture 4: Faraday turns to hydrogen, one of the two parts of water.

beats.scene: Pieces of zinc fizzing in a bottle with a tube leading to a jar
beats.summary: Hydrogen is made by putting zinc in a weak acid, and the gas is collected in a jar.

beats.scene: Soap bubbles filled with a light gas rising toward a lecture hall ceiling
beats.summary: Hydrogen is the lightest gas of all, and it lifts soap bubbles into the air.

beats.scene: An early balloon floating over Paris with a crowd watching from below
beats.summary: In 1783 two men flew over Paris in a balloon filled with hydrogen.

beats.scene: An upside-down jar with a taper inside and a flame at its mouth
beats.summary: A taper put into a jar of hydrogen goes out, but the hydrogen burns at the mouth.

beats.scene: A pale, nearly invisible flame burns at the top of a small glass tube
beats.summary: Hydrogen burns with a very pale flame that gives almost no light.

beats.scene: A cold dry glass held over a hydrogen flame, misted with drops
beats.summary: A cold glass over the flame is covered with water, the only thing that burning hydrogen makes.

beats.scene: A fine platinum wire glowing brilliantly in a pale hydrogen flame
beats.summary: A fine platinum wire in the pale flame glows brilliantly, showing again that a solid makes light.

beats.scene: A candle with a picture of tiny hydrogen and carbon pieces inside the wax
beats.summary: The wax of a candle contains hydrogen as well as carbon, and the hydrogen burns into the water that Faraday collected.

beats.scene: A small glass flask bursting with a flash beside a calm candle
beats.summary: Hydrogen mixed with air burns all at once, which is dangerous, while a candle burns gently.

beats.scene: Faraday at the start of the fifth lecture with a flask and a jar
beats.summary: Lecture 5: Faraday turns to oxygen, the other part of water and the part of the air that feeds a flame.

beats.scene: A glass flask heated over a burner, with a tube leading away
beats.summary: Oxygen is made by heating chlorate of potash with a black powder, manganese dioxide, in a flask.

beats.scene: A gas bubbling through a tube into an upside-down jar in a water trough
beats.summary: The gas bubbles through water and fills a jar standing upside down.

beats.scene: A glowing splinter bursting into flame inside a jar
beats.summary: Oxygen cannot be seen, but a glowing splinter bursts into flame in it.

beats.scene: A candle blazing with a brilliant white flame inside a jar of pure oxygen
beats.summary: A candle burns far more brightly in pure oxygen than it does in air.

beats.scene: A piece of red-hot charcoal throwing sparks in a jar of oxygen
beats.summary: Charcoal glows fiercely in oxygen and throws out sparks.

beats.scene: A dazzling white flame inside a jar, held by a spoon
beats.summary: Phosphorus burns in oxygen with a dazzling white light.

beats.scene: A pale blue flame in air beside a bright violet flame in a jar
beats.summary: Sulphur burns with a pale flame in air and a bright violet flame in oxygen.

beats.scene: A thin iron wire burning in a jar, with a shower of sparks falling
beats.summary: A thin iron wire burns in oxygen with a fierce light and a shower of sparks.

beats.scene: The Earth cut open, with rock, water and air shaded alike
beats.summary: Oxygen is found almost everywhere on Earth, in the air, in water and in rock.

beats.scene: A bottle of air divided into five parts, with one part coloured
beats.summary: The air around us is a mixture of gases, and about one fifth of it is oxygen.

beats.scene: A closed jar over water with a burning dish inside, water rising
beats.summary: Burning something in a closed jar uses up the oxygen, and water rises to fill about a fifth of the jar.

beats.scene: A grey jar of nitrogen where a burning match is put out
beats.summary: The rest of the air is mostly nitrogen, which does not burn and does not help things to burn.

beats.scene: A candle burning calmly in air beside a fierce one in oxygen
beats.summary: Nitrogen spreads the oxygen out, so that things burn steadily in air and not fiercely.

beats.scene: Two strands of different colours lying side by side, then pulled apart
beats.summary: The gases of the air are mixed, not joined, so they can be separated again.

beats.scene: A large glass bottle of air on one side of a balance scale
beats.summary: Air has weight: a litre of it weighs a little more than a gram.

beats.scene: A glass bell jar on a table, with a pump beside it
beats.summary: Faraday shows that air presses on everything, with about a kilogram on each square centimetre.

beats.scene: A hand pressed over the open end of a jar on a pump
beats.summary: When air is pumped out of a jar, a hand over its open end is pressed down firmly.

beats.scene: Children standing under a sky with arrows pushing in and out
beats.summary: We are not crushed by the air, because the air inside our bodies pushes back equally.

beats.scene: A mountain with the sky growing thinner above it and a climber panting
beats.summary: The air reaches up for many miles and grows thinner as it rises.

beats.scene: A candle burns on a table and little arrows show gases rising away
beats.summary: A burning candle seems to vanish, but nothing is lost: it turns into invisible gases that mix with the air.

beats.scene: A jar held over a flame, then shaken with limewater that turns milky
beats.summary: Air from over a flame turns clear limewater milky, so the candle makes a second gas besides water.

beats.scene: A clear glass of limewater beside a lump of white lime
beats.summary: Limewater is made by stirring a little lime into water, and lime is made by heating chalk or limestone.

beats.scene: A tube drawing air from above a candle into a bottle of limewater
beats.summary: Faraday draws more of the gas through limewater and the liquid slowly turns milky.

beats.scene: A piece of charcoal burns red in a jar and clear limewater turns white
beats.summary: Charcoal burned in oxygen makes the same gas, and it turns limewater milky in the same way.

beats.scene: A chart joining a piece of carbon with oxygen to make a gas
beats.summary: The gas comes from the carbon in the candle joining with oxygen from the air.

beats.scene: A drawing of a carbon dioxide piece with one carbon and two oxygens
beats.summary: Today the gas is called carbon dioxide, because each piece has one carbon joined to two oxygens.

beats.scene: A balance with a candle on one side and heavier gases on the other
beats.summary: The gases that a candle makes would weigh more than the candle itself, because oxygen joins them.

beats.scene: A sealed jar with a burning candle standing on a pair of scales
beats.summary: In a sealed jar, a burning candle does not change the total weight.

beats.scene: A French chemist at a laboratory table weighing small glass vessels
beats.summary: In the 1770s Lavoisier showed that burning means joining with oxygen and that nothing is lost.

beats.scene: A candle lowered into a tall jar of invisible gas goes dark
beats.summary: Faraday shows that carbon dioxide cannot help a flame to burn: a candle lowered into a jar of it goes out.

beats.scene: A jar of gas weighed on a balance beside a jar of plain air
beats.summary: Carbon dioxide is about one and a half times heavier than air.

beats.scene: A glass jar tipped as if pouring water over a small candle
beats.summary: Faraday pours the invisible gas from one jar into another, and a candle in the second jar goes out.

beats.scene: A long wooden trough with a row of candles and a jar tipped above
beats.summary: Poured down a long trough, carbon dioxide puts out a row of candles, one after another.

beats.scene: Fizzing bubbles rise from white marble in a glass of acid
beats.summary: Marble and a little acid give off carbon dioxide, which Faraday collects in jars.

beats.scene: A lime kiln with white stone inside and a plume of gas above it
beats.summary: Heating limestone in a kiln drives off carbon dioxide and leaves lime.

beats.scene: A white chalk cliff beside a seashell and a block of marble
beats.summary: Chalk, marble and seashells are made of the same stuff, and a good part of it is carbon dioxide held in solid form.

beats.scene: A bottle of fizzy water opened, with bubbles streaming to the top
beats.summary: Carbon dioxide dissolves in water, which is why soda water fizzes when the bottle is opened.

beats.scene: An old stone well with a lantern lowered on a rope
beats.summary: The heavy gas collects in low places such as old wells and brewers' vats, where it can be dangerous.

beats.scene: A red fire extinguisher beside a small fire that is going out
beats.summary: Because carbon dioxide puts out flames, it is used today in fire extinguishers.

beats.scene: A lump of charcoal glowing red in a dish with no flame above it
beats.summary: Charcoal burns with a red glow and almost no flame, because carbon does not turn into vapour first.

beats.scene: Charcoal burners tending a smoking mound of logs covered with turf
beats.summary: Charcoal is made by heating wood with very little air, so that the carbon is left behind.

beats.scene: Wood heated in a closed pot with a small flame at a pipe
beats.summary: When wood is heated without air, it gives off a vapour that burns and leaves black charcoal.

beats.scene: Coal crumbs sealed in a clay pipe bowl with gas lit at the stem
beats.summary: Faraday heats coal in a closed vessel, and a gas comes out that burns like a candle's vapour.

beats.scene: A gasworks with tall iron ovens, pipes, and heaps of black coke
beats.summary: In a gasworks coal is heated in closed ovens, and the gas is led away through pipes.

beats.scene: Heaps of coke and barrels of tar standing beside a gasworks yard
beats.summary: The gasworks also leaves coke, which burns as a fuel, and thick black tar.

beats.scene: A lamplighter with a long pole lighting a gas lamp on a London street
beats.summary: In the early 1800s London began to light its streets with coal gas.

beats.scene: A yellow gas jet on a wall beside a candle on a table
beats.summary: A gas flame shines for the same reason as a candle, because glowing carbon is in it.

beats.scene: A hot blue flame from a burner with air holes at the bottom
beats.summary: A burner that mixes air with the gas gives a hot blue flame with very little light.

beats.scene: A coal seam in a rock face with a fossil fern pressed into it
beats.summary: Coal is made from plants that grew in forests many millions of years ago.

beats.scene: Faraday blowing through a glass tube into a jar of limewater
beats.summary: Faraday breathes through a tube into limewater, and it turns milky just as it did for the candle.

beats.scene: A person's breath misting a cold glass beside a candle's flame
beats.summary: Breath also carries water vapour, which is why it clouds a cold glass.

beats.scene: Two jars of air, one fresh and one breathed in and out again
beats.summary: The air we breathe out has less oxygen and much more carbon dioxide than the air we breathe in.

beats.scene: A drawing of lungs with tiny tubes, blood vessels and arrows
beats.summary: In the lungs the air comes close to the blood, which carries oxygen to every part of the body.

beats.scene: A sugar lump melting and blackening in a spoon over a flame
beats.summary: Sugar is made of carbon, hydrogen and oxygen, and heated in a flame it blackens and leaves carbon.

beats.scene: A plate of bread, fruit and meat next to a burning candle
beats.summary: Food is the body's fuel, and its carbon joins slowly with the oxygen that we breathe in.

beats.scene: A thermometer in a person's hand reading thirty-seven degrees
beats.summary: The slow burning keeps a healthy body warm at about 37 degrees Celsius.

beats.scene: A boy running in a park, breathing hard with his chest rising
beats.summary: The harder we work, the faster we breathe and the more food our bodies need.

beats.scene: A crowded, shut room with a single candle burning low
beats.summary: In a crowded shut room the air has less oxygen and more carbon dioxide, so fresh air is needed.

beats.scene: A candle on a table and a girl beside it, breathing together
beats.summary: Faraday says that a candle's burning and a person's breathing are the same chemistry.

beats.scene: Chimneys, lamps and crowds of people under one grey sky
beats.summary: Fires and living creatures send carbon dioxide into the air all the time, yet the air stays fresh.

beats.scene: Green leaves held up to the sun with arrows pointing into them
beats.summary: Plants take in carbon dioxide through their leaves and build its carbon into their own bodies.

beats.scene: A sprig of mint in a closed glass jar with a candle beside it
beats.summary: In 1771 Joseph Priestley put a sprig of mint in air spoiled by a burning candle and found that the air became good again.

beats.scene: A Dutch doctor beside a water plant making bubbles in sunlight
beats.summary: Later, Jan Ingenhousz showed that plants need sunlight to make this change in the air.

beats.scene: A leaf in bright sun with bubbles rising and a dark leaf beside it
beats.summary: In sunlight a green leaf gives out oxygen, while in darkness it stops making it.

beats.scene: A beeswax candle, a palm and a flower in a wax-maker's workshop
beats.summary: Wax, oil and fat all come from plants, or from animals that ate plants.

beats.scene: A tall oak growing from a small acorn beside a bag of soil
beats.summary: A tree grows mostly from air and water, and only a little from the soil.

beats.scene: A glass bowl holding a goldfish and green water plants in sunlight
beats.summary: A bowl holding fish and water plants shows the same balance in a small way.

beats.scene: A circle drawn through a plant, a person, a flame and the air
beats.summary: The carbon travels in a circle from the air to plants, to us or to a flame, and back to the air.

beats.scene: A girl breathing out beside a tree with a leaf in her hand
beats.summary: The carbon in a breath may one day become part of a leaf.

beats.scene: A candle, a green plant and a child in a ring of light
beats.summary: Faraday says that the same laws govern a candle, a plant and a person, so that nature is one connected whole.

beats.scene: Three jars labelled carbon, hydrogen and oxygen, with arrows between them
beats.summary: Burning, breathing and growing are all the same few substances changing partners.

beats.scene: Faraday leaning toward the young audience with a candle at his side
beats.summary: Faraday asks the children to look carefully, to ask questions and to trust only what they have tested.

beats.scene: A child with a candle, a plate and a jar at a kitchen table
beats.summary: Many of the experiments can be repeated with a candle, a plate and a jar, if an adult helps.

beats.scene: Faraday at the lecture table with his hand near the lighted candle
beats.summary: Faraday says that the candle has taught only the first small lessons, and much remains to be discovered.

beats.scene: An audience of children looking up at the single flame on the table
beats.summary: In his last words, Faraday wishes that the children may shine like candles to all around them.

beats.scene: Six lecture titles written in a row above a single burning candle
beats.summary: In six lectures, one small flame has led the audience through fire, water, air, carbon and breath.

beats.scene: A thin printed book of 1861 lying open beside a candlestick
beats.summary: The lectures were printed as a book in 1861 from notes by William Crookes, and have been read ever since.

beats.scene: An electric generator and motor beside a portrait of Faraday
beats.summary: Faraday also made great discoveries about electricity, including the principle behind the generator and the motor.

beats.scene: A lighted candle on a table with a hand shielding the flame
beats.summary: Next time you light a candle, you can see what Faraday saw: the cup, the wick, the vapour, the glow and the unseen gases.

Fire is useful, but children must be careful and ask an adult for help.

At thirteen, Faraday worked in a shop and carried newspapers to customers.
At fourteen, he became an apprentice and learned to bind books.
Faraday read the books he bound, especially the ones about science.
He made small electrical experiments with a glass bottle and a few simple parts.
A customer gave Faraday tickets to hear the famous scientist Humphry Davy.
Faraday wrote careful notes about the lectures and bound them in a book.
In 1813, Davy asked Faraday to work with him at the Royal Institution.
In 1825, Faraday began the Christmas Lectures for young people.
Faraday shows the children candles made of many different materials.
Tallow is animal fat, and it made the cheapest candles of all.
Bees make wax to build their homes, and people make candles from it.
Some fine candles were made from a special wax found in whales.
Chemists also learned to make hard white candles from animal fat.
Cheap candles were made by dipping a wick into hot melted fat.
Poor families sometimes burned a dry plant stem dipped in fat.
Old wicks bent over and smoked, so people trimmed them with scissors.
A plaited wick curls to the edge and burns away by itself.
Long ago, people marked lines on candles to tell the time.
A match touches the wick, and a small blue flame begins to grow.
The heat melts the wax near the wick and makes a little cup.
Cool air flows past the edge, so the rim of the cup stays hard.
In a strong wind, the edge melts and the wax runs down one side.
So the candle makes its own little lamp, full of liquid fuel.
Liquid wax climbs up the wick through tiny spaces between the threads.
A sponge or a towel also pulls water up into itself.
Water climbs higher in a thin glass tube than in a wide one.
A sugar cube touching tea soon becomes wet all the way up.
Only the tip of the wick burns, because the wax keeps cooling it.
When Faraday blows out the candle, a white trail of smoke rises.
A flame held in the smoke jumps down and lights the wick again.
The wax must first melt, then turn into a gas, before it burns.
Faraday puts one end of a glass tube in the dark middle.
At the far end of the tube, the gas burns as a second flame.
A card pushed into the flame turns brown in a ring.
A fine wire net held over the flame stops the fire from rising.
Above the net, the gas burns alone, and the fire cannot pass through.
Humphry Davy used this idea to make a safe lamp for miners.
The metal takes away heat, so the gas outside the lamp cannot catch fire.
A candle flame is shaped like a tongue, tall and pointed.
Hot air rises, and cooler air flows in from below to replace it.
A bright lamp throws the shadow of the flame onto a screen.
The flame leans and shakes when a breath of wind touches it.
In the 1780s, a man named Argand made a better lamp.
His lamp has a round wick, so air reaches the flame inside.
A tall glass chimney pulls more air up and makes the flame steady.
A chimney on a fireplace works in the same way as well.
These bright, steady lamps were used in lighthouses and in many homes.
Faraday ends the lecture by reminding the children what they have seen.
In the second lecture, Faraday asks why a candle flame shines.
A spirit lamp burns with a pale flame that gives little light.
Faraday says a bright flame holds tiny pieces of something solid.
A thin platinum wire in a pale flame glows brightly.
Iron filings thrown into a flame burn in bright, dancing sparks.
A fine powder blown through a flame makes a great flash of light.
A blacksmith's iron glows red, then yellow, then white as it gets hotter.
A hot coal glows brightly even when it has no flame.
Inside the candle flame, the heat makes tiny black bits of carbon.
The tiny bits glow and then burn away, so the flame stays clean.
Faraday holds a cold white plate in the flame, and it turns black.
The black powder is soot, and it is almost pure carbon.
Camphor is a white solid that burns with a very smoky flame.
Turpentine, made from pine trees, also burns with thick black smoke.
These flames have more carbon than the air can burn at once.
A good candle makes no smoke, because all its carbon burns.
A lamp wick turned up too high makes smoke instead of light.
In Faraday's London, coal fires filled the air with black smoke.
Soot can also be used to make black ink and paint.
When carbon burns cleanly, it disappears, and Faraday asks where it goes.
When a glass jar covers the candle, the flame grows dim and dies.
The jar is still full of air, but the candle cannot use it.
A candle burns well in an open bottle but not in a closed one.
A candle lowered into a tall jar burns smaller and smaller.
A blacksmith blows air onto a fire to make it hotter.
If the air is shut off, an Argand lamp makes only smoke.
A stove burns fast when its door is open and slow when shut.
A big jar lets a candle burn longer than a small jar.
Faraday says that the flame uses only one part of the air.
The second lecture ends, and Faraday says that burning also makes something new.
In the third lecture, Faraday asks what a burning candle makes.
A cold shiny cup held over the flame is soon covered with drops.
Ice and salt make a mixture that is colder than ice alone.
Drops from the cold cup run together into a clear liquid.
A warm cup stays dry, because the water stays as invisible steam.
Water can be ice, liquid water or steam, but it is always water.
When water freezes, it grows larger and can burst a bottle.
Steam is invisible, and the cloud above a kettle is tiny drops.
The sun lifts water from the sea, and it falls again as rain.
Faraday says that a candle makes water as it burns.
Potassium is a soft silver metal that must be kept under oil.
When Faraday drops it on water, it bursts into a purple flame.
It burns the same way on the drops from the candle.
In 1807, Humphry Davy used electricity to make potassium for the first time.
The metal takes something out of the water, and that gas burns.
Hot iron can also take something out of steam.
In 1800, Volta made the first battery from metal and wet cloth.
When Faraday puts two battery wires into water, gas bubbles rise.
One tube fills with twice as much gas as the other tube.
Later, Faraday measured exactly how much electricity this kind of work needs.
In the fourth lecture, Faraday looks at one part of water.
Faraday makes a gas by putting zinc in a weak acid.
Hydrogen is the lightest gas, and it lifts soap bubbles up.
In 1783, people flew in a balloon filled with hydrogen over Paris.
A candle put into hydrogen goes out, but the hydrogen burns.
Hydrogen burns with a pale flame that gives almost no light.
A cold glass over the flame gets wet, and that is pure water.
A bit of wire in the pale flame glows brightly.
The wax of a candle holds hydrogen as well as carbon.
Hydrogen mixed with air burns all at once, so it is dangerous.
In the fifth lecture, Faraday talks about oxygen, the other part of water.
He heats a white powder with a black one in a glass flask.
The gas bubbles through water into a jar, and the jar fills.
Oxygen has no colour or smell, but a glowing stick bursts into flame in it.
A candle lowered into oxygen burns with a brilliant white flame.
Charcoal glows fiercely in oxygen and throws out bright sparks.
A tiny piece of phosphorus burns in oxygen with a dazzling light.
Sulphur burns with a pale flame in air and a bright one in oxygen.
Even a thin iron wire burns in oxygen, with a shower of sparks.
There is more oxygen in the world than any other element.
Air is a mixture of gases, and about one fifth is oxygen.
Burning inside a closed jar uses up the oxygen and nothing else.
The rest of the air is mostly nitrogen, which does not burn.
A burning match goes out in a jar of pure nitrogen.
Nitrogen keeps burning slow and calm, so fires do not rage.
Air has weight, and a big bottle of air can be weighed.
The air presses on everything, with about a kilogram on each square centimetre.
When air is pumped from a jar, a hand on top is pushed down hard.
We are not crushed, because the air inside our bodies pushes back.
The air reaches up for many miles, and it grows thinner as it rises.

Limewater is clear water with a little lime mixed in.
Faraday pulls the air from a flame through limewater, and it turns milky.
Burning charcoal in oxygen makes the same gas, and limewater turns milky.
So the gas comes from the carbon in the candle.

In a closed jar, a burning candle does not change the weight.
Lavoisier showed that burning means joining with oxygen from the air.
A candle in a jar of this gas goes out.
This gas is heavier than air, about one and a half times.

He pours the gas down a trough, and the candles go out.

The gas dissolves in water, so soda water makes bubbles.
The heavy gas can collect at the bottom of old wells.
Today, fire fighters use this gas to put out some fires.

Food is fuel, and it slowly joins with the oxygen we breathe.
