B1B2: In a lecture hall at the Royal Institution in London, Michael Faraday placed a single candle on his table. He told the children in front of him that this simple thing was a door to all of nature.

Each Christmas, the Royal Institution in London invites young people to a series of talks on science, with real experiments to watch. Faraday loved this tradition, and he gave the series himself that winter.
On Faraday's long table stood glass jars, tubes, a small burner and a trough of water. He liked to use simple things that his audience could see and understand.
Faraday said that he had chosen the candle as his subject, and that its story was a chemical one. A candle may seem a very small thing, but he promised that it would take them a long way.

He put three simple questions to the children, and he wrote them where everyone could see. How does the wax get up to the flame, why does the flame shine, and what becomes of the candle when it burns away?
In total there would be six lectures, and each one would answer questions raised by the one before. They would begin with the flame itself and end with the way that we breathe.
Faraday asked his audience to watch closely and to ask questions about everything they saw. He wanted them to understand what was happening, and not merely to enjoy the show.
In 1848, most homes in Britain were lit by candles and oil lamps, and gas lit the streets of the big cities. The candle was so common that hardly anyone stopped to wonder how it worked.
Look at the flame, Faraday said, and you will see that it is not one colour. It is bright yellow at the top, blue near the bottom, and dark in the middle.
Fire is a good servant but a bad master, as the old saying goes. Anyone who repeats these experiments should do so only with an adult beside them.
Michael Faraday was born on 22 September 1791 in a village south of London that is now part of the city. His father, James, was a blacksmith who often had little money and was sometimes ill.

The Faraday family was poor, and Michael had only a few years of schooling, in which he learned to read, write and do simple sums. It is said that at one hard time a single loaf of bread had to last him a whole week.

At the age of thirteen, Michael found work as an errand boy for George Riebau, a bookseller and bookbinder in London. Part of his job was to deliver newspapers to customers and to collect them again, since the shop lent them out.
A year later, Michael became Riebau's apprentice and began to learn the trade of bookbinding. The apprenticeship was to last seven years, and in that time he would stitch and cover many books.

While he was binding books in the shop, Michael often stopped to read some of them. Two of them changed his life: an article on electricity in an encyclopaedia, and a book called Conversations on Chemistry, written by Jane Marcet.
Michael was not content merely to read about science, and he began to try out what he had read. With a glass bottle and a few simple parts, he built a small machine that made electricity.
In 1812, a customer named William Dance gave Michael tickets to four lectures by the famous chemist Humphry Davy. Michael sat in the crowded hall of the Royal Institution and listened to every word.

Michael wrote careful notes during the lectures and then copied them out neatly, with drawings, into a book of about three hundred pages. He bound the book himself and sent it to Davy, hoping for a job in science.

Davy was impressed, and in March 1813 he hired Michael as his assistant at the Royal Institution. Later that year they set out together on a long tour of Europe, where the young man met many famous scientists.
Faraday worked hard at the Royal Institution and became one of the great scientists of his age. In 1825 he began the Christmas Lectures for young people, which are still given there today.
In the first lecture, Faraday set out candles made from several different materials, so that everyone could see how much they varied. Some were yellowish, some pale and some almost pure white.
Tallow, the fat of cattle and sheep, was the cheapest candle material of all. It melts easily and often smells strong, but it kept many ordinary homes lit for centuries.
Beeswax comes from honeybees, who make it to build the walls of their honeycomb. Candles made from it burn cleanly and slowly, and they give off a faint, sweet smell.
Spermaceti is a pale wax taken from the head of the sperm whale. It was very expensive, and it made fine, hard candles that burned with a bright, steady flame.

In the 1820s, the French chemist Michel Chevreul helped to find a way to separate the hard part of animal fat, which is called stearin. Candles made from it were harder, cleaner and less smelly than tallow candles.
Many candles were made by dipping a wick into hot melted fat again and again. Each dip added a thin coat, until the candle was as thick as it was meant to be.
Poor families sometimes made their own light from a rush, a thin dry plant stem, dipped in fat. A rushlight gave only a weak glow, but it cost almost nothing.
At the heart of every candle is a wick, which is usually made of twisted cotton threads. Old tallow wicks tended to bend over and smoke, so people trimmed them often with a pair of snuffers.
A plaited wick is woven so that it curls over as it burns. The tip then reaches the outer edge of the flame, where it burns away, and nobody has to trim it.
Before clocks were common, people sometimes marked lines on a candle to tell the time. As the wax burned down past each line, another hour had gone by.
When Faraday touched a match to the wick, only a small blue flame appeared at first. It grew larger and brighter over the next minute, as the heat melted more wax around it.
The heat of the flame melts the wax near the wick, and the liquid gathers in a little cup. Faraday asked his audience to look at it closely, because the shape of the cup is no accident.
The rim of the cup stays solid, because the air that rushes up toward the flame also cools the outside of the candle. That is why the cup holds its liquid wax like a small bowl made of wax itself.
In a draught, the air no longer flows evenly, and one side of the rim is not cooled properly. The wax there melts, overflows and runs down the side of the candle, which wastes fuel.
In this way a candle is really a lamp that makes its own bowl. The solid wax turns to liquid in the cup, and the liquid is the fuel that feeds the flame.

The liquid wax then climbs up the wick, as if something were pulling it. This happens because the wick is made of many fine threads with tiny spaces between them, and the liquid creeps into those spaces.
A sponge does the same thing when you dip a corner of it in water, and so does the corner of a towel. The water climbs up into it, far above the level of the pool below.
The thinner a glass tube is, the higher water will climb up inside it. Faraday called this action capillary attraction, from a Latin word for hair, because the narrowest tubes are as fine as a hair.
You can see the same thing with a lump of sugar touching the edge of a cup of tea. The tea soon creeps up through the sugar until the whole lump is wet.

Only the tip of the wick burns, because the wax that keeps flowing up it also keeps it from getting too hot. If the wick is too thick, it brings up more fuel than the flame can burn, and the flame begins to smoke.
Faraday blew out the candle, and a white trail of smoke curled up from the wick. He told the children to watch it closely, because it was about to teach them something.
He held a lighted taper in the white trail, a little way above the wick. The flame ran down the trail and lit the wick again, which showed that the white smoke could burn.
Faraday now explained the long journey that the fuel makes inside a burning candle. The solid wax first melts into a liquid, then the liquid turns into a vapour, and it is the vapour that burns.
To prove that the flame holds vapour, Faraday pushed one end of a thin glass tube into its dark middle. White vapour travelled along the tube, just as smoke travels along a chimney.

He bent the tube so that its far end was a little way from the candle, and he lit the vapour that came out. It burned at the end of the tube like a second small candle, while the first flame carried on burning.
Faraday pressed a piece of card flat across a flame for a moment. It turned brown in a ring, which showed that the burning takes place at the outside of the flame and not in its hollow middle.
Next Faraday held a piece of fine wire gauze, which is like a very fine metal net, down over the flame. The flame could not pass through it, and the gauze held it back like a closed door.
When he lit the smoke above the gauze, it burned there as a second flame. The fire did not travel down through the metal, and the candle below was left alone.
Humphry Davy used this very idea to make a safe lamp for coal miners in 1815. Before then, the naked flame of a miner's candle could set fire to explosive gas in the mine.
The metal of the gauze carries the heat away so quickly that the gas outside cannot catch fire. Davy chose not to take out a patent on his lamp, so that any mine could use it freely.
In still air, the flame of a candle is shaped like a tongue, tall and narrow with a pointed tip. Faraday said that this shape tells us something about the air around the flame.

The flame heats the air near it, and hot air is lighter than cold air, so it rises. Cooler air rushes in from below to take its place, and this makes a steady stream of air moving upward past the flame.

To make the stream of air visible, Faraday shone a bright lamp so that the candle's shadow fell on a screen. Above the flame, the rising hot air showed itself as a dark, wavering ribbon in the shadow.
A gentle breath or a draught pushes the flame sideways, and then it flickers and changes shape. Only in perfectly still air does a flame keep its calm and graceful tongue.
In the 1780s, a Swiss scientist named Argand invented a lamp that gave a much better light than a candle. Its wick was woven into a hollow ring instead of a flat strip.
Air could reach this ring-shaped flame from two sides, from outside the ring and through its hollow middle. With so much air, the fuel burned fully and gave a bright, steady light.
Argand's burner was fitted with a tall glass chimney. The hot air rises up the glass, which draws a strong, steady stream of fresh air in at the bottom.
A chimney over a fire in a house works in just the same way. The hot air and smoke rise up it, and fresh air is pulled into the room to feed the fire.
Lamps like Argand's were much brighter than candles, and they became popular in homes, shops and lighthouses. Light for reading and for working had become easier to come by.

With that, the first lecture came to its end, and the audience went home with plenty to think about. They had learned that the fuel melts, climbs the wick, turns to vapour and burns, while fresh air feeds the flame.
In the second lecture, Faraday began by reminding the children of what they had learned the day before. Then he asked a new question: why does the flame of a candle shine so brightly?
He pointed out that not every flame gives a good light, and that some flames are very dim indeed. A spirit lamp, which burns alcohol, makes a pale blue flame that lights a room hardly at all.
Faraday suggested that a bright flame must have something in it that shines. He believed that this was solid matter, in the form of tiny particles, because solid things glow when they are hot.
He held a thin platinum wire in the pale flame of the spirit lamp, and it glowed brightly at once. The wire was a solid, and the heat made it shine, although the flame itself gave almost no light.
Next he sprinkled a pinch of fine iron filings into a flame. Each tiny piece caught fire and burned with a bright spark, so that the flame became full of glittering light.
Faraday then blew a little lycopodium powder through a flame. This light yellow powder, made from the spores of a plant, burned all at once in a great flash, like a small bolt of lightning.
Any solid thing will begin to glow if it is made hot enough. A blacksmith like Faraday's father sees iron glow dull red when it is warm, then orange, and then almost white as it gets hotter.
A glowing coal in a fire shows the same thing. It may have no flame of its own, yet it shines red because it is a solid that has been made very hot.
So where do the solid pieces in a candle flame come from? Inside the flame, the heat breaks the wax vapour apart and sets free countless tiny particles of black carbon.
These tiny particles glow white hot, and they give the flame nearly all of its light. As they reach the edge of the flame, they meet the air and burn away, and so a clean flame leaves no soot behind.
Faraday held a cold white saucer in the flame of the candle for a moment. When he took it away, the bottom of the saucer was covered with a layer of black soot.
This soot is carbon, the same black stuff that is found in charcoal. Faraday told the children that even the sparkling diamond is made of carbon, which is one of the great surprises of chemistry.
Some materials make far more soot than a candle does. Camphor, a white waxy solid that comes from a tree, burns with a thick and very smoky flame.
Turpentine, which is made from the sap of pine trees, does the same. When it was set alight in a dish, black clouds of smoke rolled up into the air.
These flames smoke because they hold more carbon than the air can burn up at once. The carbon that is left over escapes unburned and floats away as black smoke.
A candle burns without smoke because its flame gets just enough air to burn all the carbon. The tiny black particles glow, then burn up completely, and nothing is left to drift away.
You can see this in a lamp with a wick that can be raised and lowered. If the wick is turned too high, the flame suddenly begins to smoke, and turning it down puts it right again.
In Faraday's London, thousands of coal fires and chimneys filled the air with smoke. Buildings were darkened with soot, and on bad days a thick brown fog hung over the streets.
Fine black soot, which is called lampblack, has long been used to make black ink and paint. So even the smoke of a lamp can be put to good use.
Faraday ended this part of the lecture with a question for the children to think about. If a clean flame burns up all its carbon, he asked, where does that carbon go?
Faraday placed a glass jar over a burning candle. The flame grew smaller and dimmer, and after a short time it went out.
The jar was still full of air, and yet the candle could no longer burn in it. Faraday explained that the air must have been changed by the burning, so that it could not keep the flame alive.
He then put two candles in two bottles, one open at the top and one closed with a cork. The candle in the open bottle burned brightly, while the one in the closed bottle soon sank low and went out.
He lowered a burning candle on a wire into a tall glass jar. At first it burned well, but as it went deeper the flame grew weaker, until at last it could not burn at all.
A blacksmith, like Faraday's father, makes a fire hotter by blowing air through it with a pair of bellows. The more air the fire is given, the faster the fuel burns and the brighter it glows.

Faraday also used the Argand lamp to show how much a flame depends on its air. When the air that goes up through the middle of the flame was shut off, the flame turned dull and began to give out smoke.
A stove or a fire in a grate works in the same way. If its door and air vents are opened, it burns fiercely, and if they are closed, it burns low and slowly.
A big jar lets a candle burn for longer than a small jar does, because it holds more air. This shows that a candle uses up something in the air as it burns.
Yet the candle does not use all of the air in the jar. Faraday explained that only one part of the air keeps a flame alive, and that the rest does nothing to help it.

That was the end of the second lecture, and the children had learned a great deal. Faraday told them that burning makes something new as well as using up air, and that next time they would find out what.
At the start of the third lecture, Faraday asked a new question: what does a burning candle make? The air that is left in a jar is changed, and he wanted to know what had been added to it.
He held a shiny, cold cup over the flame of a candle. Very soon the outside of the cup was clouded with tiny drops that ran together and trickled down.

To catch more of the drops, Faraday filled a metal vessel with ice and salt, which makes a mixture much colder than ice alone. He held the vessel over a flame, and drops of water gathered on its cold sides and fell into a dish.
The drops ran together into a small pool of clear liquid with no colour and no smell. It looked like water, and Faraday said that it was water, but he wanted to prove it beyond doubt.
A warm cup, by contrast, stays dry above a flame. The water is still there, but it remains in the air as an invisible vapour until something cold makes it gather into drops.

Water is a wonderful substance, because it can be ice, liquid water or steam, and it is still the same stuff in each form. Faraday showed all three, with a block of ice, a glass of water and a kettle.
When water freezes, it expands, and it can burst a bottle or a pipe if it has no room to grow. That is why water pipes sometimes break in a hard winter.
Steam itself is a gas, and like most gases it cannot be seen at all. The white cloud above a kettle is made of tiny drops that have cooled, which is why there is a clear gap at the spout.
Rain falls on the hills and flows down the rivers to the sea. The sun then lifts water from the sea into the air again, clouds form, and the great cycle goes on.
Faraday told the children that a burning candle makes water too, a little at a time. Yet it was one thing to say so, and quite another to prove that the drops really came from the flame.
Faraday took out a lump of potassium, a soft, silvery metal that has to be kept under oil. It is so soft that it can be cut with a knife, and the fresh cut shines for only a moment.

He dropped a small piece of the metal onto a dish of water in front of the audience. It skated across the surface and burst into a lilac flame, which is what potassium always does when it meets water.
Then he dropped a piece into the drops that he had caught from the candle. It burned in exactly the same way, and that proved that the liquid from the flame really was water.

Potassium is not found as a metal in nature, and for a long time nobody had seen it. Humphry Davy made it for the first time in 1807, by sending a strong electric current through a substance called potash.
The potassium takes something away from the water, and the gas that is set free is what burns. The lilac colour of the flame belongs to the potassium itself.
Faraday also heated some iron in a tube and passed steam over it. The iron took something from the steam and turned black, and a gas came out of the tube that could be lit.
A battery gives a steady flow of electricity, and the first one was made by Alessandro Volta in Italy in 1800. It was a pile of metal discs separated by pieces of damp cloth.
Faraday connected two wires from a battery to a dish of water. Bubbles of gas rose from the wires and were collected in two glass tubes, one for each wire.
One tube filled with twice as much gas as the other. The two gases were quite different, which showed that water is made of two things joined together.

Faraday later studied the link between electricity and chemistry very closely, and he helped to invent words such as electrode and ion. It was a long way from the water in the candle, but it began with the same simple experiment.

In the fourth lecture, Faraday said that the water made by the candle must be looked at more closely. Water, as the battery had shown, is made of two things, and the first of these is called hydrogen.

To make hydrogen, Faraday put pieces of zinc in a bottle and added a weak acid. The metal fizzed, and a gas bubbled out of the bottle and was collected in a jar, though this is work for a trained chemist.
Hydrogen is the lightest gas of all, about fourteen times lighter than air. Soap bubbles filled with it rise up to the ceiling, as Faraday showed with a bubble that floated up and burst.
Because hydrogen is so light, it was used in the first balloons. In December 1783, two men rose over Paris in a balloon filled with hydrogen, and they landed safely after about two hours in the air.
Faraday held a jar of hydrogen with its mouth pointing down and pushed a lighted taper up into it. The hydrogen caught fire at the mouth of the jar, but the taper went out as it went further in.
Hydrogen burns with a very pale flame that gives almost no light. This fits Faraday's idea, because there are no solid particles in it to glow.
When a cold, dry glass was held over the hydrogen flame, drops of water quickly formed on it. Burning one kilogram of hydrogen makes nine kilograms of water, because oxygen from the air joins it.
Faraday held a fine platinum wire in the pale flame, and it glowed brilliantly. It was a second proof that a flame shines when it has solid matter in it, and not merely when it is hot.
The wax of a candle holds hydrogen as well as carbon. When the wax burns, the carbon makes the light, and the hydrogen burns to make the water that Faraday collected.
Hydrogen mixed with air burns almost all at once, with a sharp bang, and so it is dangerous in the wrong hands. A candle burns calmly because its fuel comes off the melted wax a little at a time.
In the fifth lecture, Faraday turned to the other part of water, which is called oxygen. Chemists first made it in the 1770s, and it was found to be the part of the air that keeps a flame alive.

To make oxygen, Faraday heated a white powder called chlorate of potash together with a black powder called manganese dioxide in a flask. The black powder helps the white one to give up its oxygen, and it is not used up itself.
A tube carried the gas from the flask into a jar full of water that stood upside down in a trough. The gas bubbled up into the jar and pushed the water out, until the jar was full of oxygen.
Oxygen has no colour, taste or smell, and it cannot be seen. Yet when Faraday pushed a glowing splinter into the jar, it burst into flame at once, which proved that oxygen was there.
A candle lowered into a jar of oxygen burned far more brilliantly than it does in air. The flame grew larger and whiter, and it gave out a dazzling light.
Faraday then lowered a piece of red-hot charcoal into the oxygen. It glowed fiercely and threw out bright sparks, though in air it had only glowed a dull red.

A tiny piece of phosphorus, which a trained chemist handles with great care, was lit and lowered into the jar. It burned with such a dazzling white light that the audience could hardly bear to look at it.
Sulphur burns with a small, pale blue flame in air. In oxygen, the same sulphur burns with a bright violet flame and gives off a sharp, choking smell.
A thin iron wire, which can hardly be made to burn in air, burns well in a jar of oxygen. When one end was heated and lowered into the jar, the wire burned with a fierce light and a shower of sparks.
Oxygen is found almost everywhere on Earth, and we meet it every minute of our lives. It is in the air and in water, and it makes up nearly half the weight of the rocks of the Earth's crust.
The air around us is not one gas but a mixture of gases. About one fifth of it is oxygen, and Faraday explained that this is the part that keeps a flame alive.
Chemists can show how much oxygen the air holds by burning something in a closed jar that stands over water. The burning uses up the oxygen, and the water rises to fill about one fifth of the jar.
The rest of the air is mostly a gas called nitrogen. A lighted match plunged into pure nitrogen goes out at once, because nitrogen does not burn and does not help other things to burn.
Nitrogen may seem useless, but it has an important job. It spreads the oxygen out, so that things burn steadily in air and not fiercely, as they do in pure oxygen.
The two gases in the air are only mixed together, not joined. Because of that, they can be separated again, and today the oxygen is taken from the air for use in hospitals and in industry.
Air may seem to be nothing, but it has weight. A litre of air weighs a little more than a gram, and a big room full of it weighs as much as a person.
Because air has weight, the whole sky presses down on everything beneath it. At sea level, the pressure is about the weight of a kilogram on every square centimetre.
Faraday showed the strength of this pressure with an air pump and a glass jar. When the air was pumped out of a tall jar, the hand that covered its open end was pressed down firmly by the air above.

We do not feel the air pressing on us, because the air inside our bodies pushes back with equal force. It is only when the balance is upset that we notice, as our ears do when we drive up a steep hill.

The air stretches upward for many miles, growing thinner as it rises. On a high mountain there is so little air that climbers must breathe harder, and the highest peaks are hard to climb without extra oxygen.
A candle burns away, and the wax seems to vanish. Faraday told the children that nothing is really lost, because it all turns into invisible gases that mix with the air.

Faraday held a jar over the flame for a while and then added some clear limewater and shook it. The limewater turned milky white, which showed that the candle had made a second gas, quite different from water.
Limewater is made by stirring a little lime into water and letting it settle until the water is clear. Lime itself is made by heating chalk or limestone in a very hot fire.

To collect more of the gas, Faraday drew the air from above a burning candle through a tube into a bottle of limewater. It bubbled through the liquid, and the limewater slowly turned the colour of milk.
Faraday then burned a piece of charcoal in a jar of oxygen. When he shook the jar with limewater, the limewater turned milky in exactly the same way.
Charcoal is almost pure carbon, so the milky limewater showed that the gas comes from carbon joining with oxygen. The candle, which holds a great deal of carbon, makes the very same gas as it burns.
In Faraday's day the gas was called carbonic acid, but we now call it carbon dioxide. The name means that every tiny piece of it has one atom of carbon joined to two atoms of oxygen.

When the candle burns, the oxygen from the air joins with its carbon and its hydrogen. That is why the gases that a candle makes would weigh more than the candle itself, if we could catch and weigh them all.

In chemistry, nothing is ever truly lost when something burns, although it may change its form completely. If a candle burned in a sealed jar that was weighed before and after, the weight would be exactly the same.
The French chemist Antoine Lavoisier worked this out in the 1770s and 1780s. He showed that burning is the joining of a fuel with oxygen from the air, and that nothing is lost in the process.
Faraday lowered a burning candle into a tall jar of carbon dioxide. The flame went out at once, because this gas cannot help anything to burn.
Faraday explained that carbon dioxide is much heavier than air. A jar of it weighs about one and a half times as much as a jar of ordinary air.
Because the gas is heavy, it can be poured like water, although nobody can see it. Faraday tipped one jar over another, and a candle standing in the lower jar went out.

Faraday placed a row of small candles along the bottom of a long wooden trough. When he poured the invisible gas down the trough, the flames went out one after another, starting from the end where the gas arrived.
Next he dropped some pieces of white marble into a glass vessel of weak acid. The marble fizzed and bubbled, and the gas that rose from it was the same gas that a candle makes.
Lime is made in great kilns, where heat drives the carbon dioxide out of limestone. What is left behind is quicklime, and the limewater of the earlier tests is made from it.
Chalk, marble and many seashells are all made of the same substance. A large part of that substance is carbon dioxide, which is held tightly in a solid form.
Carbon dioxide also dissolves in water, especially when it is squeezed in under pressure. That is why a bottle of soda water hisses and sparkles with bubbles when the top is taken off.
Because the gas is heavy, it sinks and gathers in low places, such as old wells and the vats of brewers. Anyone who goes down into such a place can be in danger, because a person cannot breathe it.
The same gas that is made by a candle can therefore be used to put out a fire. Many modern fire extinguishers are filled with carbon dioxide for exactly this reason.
Faraday showed the children a piece of charcoal burning with a red glow and almost no flame. Charcoal does not turn into a vapour when it is heated, so there is no vapour above it to burn.
Charcoal is made by heating wood with very little air, so that only the carbon is left. Charcoal burners used to pile logs in a mound, cover it with turf and let it smoulder slowly for days.

When wood is heated without air, it gives off a smoky vapour, and this vapour can be lit like the vapour of a candle. What remains in the pot is black, light and brittle, and it is nearly pure carbon.
Faraday packed some small pieces of coal into a clay pipe, sealed the bowl and heated it in a fire. A gas came out of the stem of the pipe, and when it was lit, it burned like the vapour of a candle.
In a gasworks, coal is heated in great closed ovens, and the gas that it gives off is led away through pipes. It is cleaned and stored, and then it travels under the streets to the lamps of the town.

The coal that stays in the ovens becomes coke, a hard, grey fuel that burns with little smoke. The gasworks also gives a thick black tar, which was a nuisance at first but later became useful for many things.
In the early years of the 1800s, London began to light its streets with coal gas. Lamplighters went from post to post at dusk, and the dark and dangerous streets became far brighter and safer.
A gas jet looks very different from a candle, but it shines for the same reason. Tiny pieces of carbon are set free in the flame, and they glow white hot before they burn away.

Later, a burner designed by the German chemist Robert Bunsen mixed air with the gas before it was lit. The flame became hot and blue and gave little light, because the carbon burned at once instead of glowing.

Coal is made from plants that grew in great forests many millions of years ago. Over a very long time, the dead trees and ferns were buried and pressed, and they slowly turned into the black rock that we burn.
Faraday took a glass tube and breathed gently through it into a jar of clear limewater. The limewater turned milky white, in exactly the same way as it did for the gas from the candle.
A person's breath carries water as well as carbon dioxide, and anyone can see this by breathing on a cold glass. The glass clouds over with tiny drops, just as the cold cup did over the flame.
The air that we breathe out is different from the air that we breathe in. It has less oxygen in it and much more carbon dioxide, which is the same gas that a candle makes.

Air travels down into the lungs, where it comes very close to the blood through walls that are extremely thin. The blood takes up oxygen there and carries it round the body, and it brings carbon dioxide back to be breathed out.

Sugar is made of carbon, hydrogen and oxygen, and Faraday showed what happens when it is heated in a flame. It melts and turns black, which shows that the carbon is there, even though a lump of sugar looks pure white.
Faraday said that the food we eat is the fuel of the body, whose carbon joins slowly with the oxygen that we breathe in. The carbon dioxide that is made is carried out of the body in the breath.
This slow burning inside us gives out heat, which is why a healthy body stays warm even on a cold day. The normal temperature of the body is about 37 degrees Celsius, and it hardly changes at all.

When a person runs or works hard, the body needs more energy, so the breathing becomes faster and deeper. That is also why people who do hard work, or who grow quickly, need more food than people who sit still.
In a shut room full of people, the air slowly changes as everyone breathes it in and out. It has less oxygen and more carbon dioxide than before, and it soon feels heavy, so fresh air is needed.

Faraday told the children that the burning of a candle and the breathing of a person are really the same thing. The candle burns in the open air, but breathing happens quietly inside us, and the two work in the same way.

Every fire, every lamp and every living creature sends carbon dioxide into the air, and they have done so for ages. Faraday asked the children why the air does not become poisoned by it, and the answer lay with the plants.

Plants take carbon dioxide from the air through their leaves, and they build its carbon into their own stems, leaves and fruit. The plant is, in a way, made out of the air that the candle and the breath have sent into it.

In 1771 the English chemist Joseph Priestley placed a sprig of mint in a jar of air that had been spoiled by a burning candle. After some days the air was good again, and a candle could be lit in it once more.

Some years later, the Dutch doctor Jan Ingenhousz found that plants can only do this when sunlight falls on them. His experiments showed that the green leaves are doing important work, and that the light is needed to do it.

In bright sunlight, a green leaf takes in carbon dioxide and gives out oxygen, and tiny bubbles can be seen rising from water plants. In the dark the leaf stops making oxygen, which is why the light matters so much.

The wax, oil and fat of which candles are made come from plants, or from animals that have fed on plants. Even the candle that Faraday lit was, in this sense, once part of a living thing and the sunlight that fell on it.

A tall tree grows mostly from the air and from water, and only a small part of it comes from the soil. When a log burns in a fire, the carbon that it gives back to the air is the carbon that the tree once took.

Anyone can see the same balance in a bowl that holds a few fish and some green water plants in the light. The fish breathe out carbon dioxide, and the plants use it and give back the oxygen that the fish need.

So the carbon moves in a great circle, from the air into plants, then into animals and people or a flame. It goes back to the air again, and it is never used up, only passed on from one thing to another.
The carbon dioxide in one breath may one day become part of a leaf, and that leaf may feed an animal. A simple breath is therefore a tiny part of the great circle of life.
Faraday told the children that the same laws govern a candle, a plant and a person. Nature, he said, is one connected whole, and a single flame can lead us to understand it.
Burning, breathing and growing all turn out to be the same few substances changing partners. Carbon, hydrogen and oxygen join and part, and they move through candles, plants and people.
Faraday asked the children to look at everything with care and to question what they saw. They were to trust only what they had tested for themselves, even when a famous person said otherwise.
Many of the experiments in the lectures are simple enough to repeat at home. Anyone can try them with a candle, a plate and a jar, but a grown-up must always stand close by.
Faraday said that the candle had taught only the first small lessons about nature. Much more remained to be discovered, and he hoped that the children would one day find it.
At the end of the last lecture, Faraday said that he hoped the children would be like candles. He wished that they would shine as lights to everyone around them and do their duty to other people.
By the end of the six lectures, one small flame had led the children through fire, water, air, carbon and breath. Nothing grand had been needed, only a table, some glass and a lighted candle.
The lectures were printed as a book in 1861, from notes that William Crookes took while Faraday spoke. The book has been read all over the world ever since, and it is still in print today.
Faraday also made great discoveries about electricity, and he found the idea behind the electric motor and the generator. The farad, a unit used in electricity, is named after him.
Next time you light a candle, you can see what Faraday saw: the cup, the wick, the vapour, the glow and the unseen gases. Small things can lead to big ideas, if we look with care.
C1C2: In a crowded lecture hall at the Royal Institution in London, the scientist Michael Faraday set a single candle on the table before an audience of eager young people. He told them, with the confidence of a man who had studied it for many years, that there was no better door into the study of nature than the burning of a candle. Every law that governs the universe, he promised, is somewhere to be found in that small flame.

Every Christmas, the Royal Institution in London threw open its doors to young people, offering them a series of lectures in which real experiments took the place of dull recitation. Faraday, who cherished the tradition and had helped to begin it, took his turn at the lectern that winter. He had no wish to dazzle his audience with mystery; he meant to explain, and he trusted children to follow.

Faraday's long table stood crowded with the plain tools of the chemist: glass jars, bent tubes, a trough of water and one small burner. Nothing on it was costly, rare or hard to understand, and that was exactly the point of the whole display. He wanted his listeners to feel that the wonders he promised sprang from ordinary things, not from clever machinery.

Having named his subject, the chemical history of a candle, Faraday admitted that it might seem too humble a thing to deserve six whole lectures. He promised, however, that it would repay their attention many times over, and that no one would leave the hall disappointed. Few ordinary objects, he suggested, lead so quickly to so many of the great questions of science.

Before the first experiment, Faraday set out three questions on which the whole course would turn. How does the solid wax find its way up to the flame, what makes that flame shine so brightly, and what becomes of the candle as it burns away? By the end of the sixth lecture, he said, each of them would have an answer.

The course was to run to six lectures, each one building on the last, like the steps of a careful argument. It would begin with the flame itself, move on to the water and the air that burning needs and makes, and end with something very close to home, the breath of everyone in the room. A single thread of reasoning, Faraday hoped, would bind all six lectures together into one connected story.

Faraday urged his young listeners to look hard at everything he showed them and to ask questions without shame. He cared less that they should remember his experiments than that they should understand what each one meant. A child who has learned to wonder why, he believed, has already begun to be a scientist.

In 1848, most homes in Britain were lit by candles and oil lamps, while gas lit the streets of the larger cities. The candle was so common, so cheap and so familiar that hardly anyone ever stopped to ask how it worked. It was precisely this ordinariness that made it, in Faraday's eyes, the perfect teacher.

Faraday invited the children to look closely at the flame itself, which is not one colour but several. At the top it is a bright and glowing yellow, near the base it has a band of blue, and in the middle there is a dark and hollow-looking space. Every one of those colours, he promised, had a reason, and the reasons would take six lectures to unfold.

Fire, as the old saying goes, is a good servant but a bad master, and Faraday never forgot it in his laboratory. The experiments in these lectures were carried out by a trained chemist with the proper equipment, so a young reader should repeat only the simplest of them, and always with a grown-up close by. Careful hands and clear thinking, after all, were as much a part of his teaching as any discovery.

Michael Faraday was born on 22 September 1791 in Newington Butts, then a village just south of London and now part of the city itself. His father, James, was a blacksmith whose health was poor and whose wages were small. It was hardly the kind of beginning that anyone would have linked with a famous career in science.

The Faraday family knew real hardship, and Michael's schooling amounted to little more than reading, writing and a little arithmetic. It is said that, in one bad year, a single loaf of bread had to last him an entire week. Whatever he lacked in money and learning, however, he made up for in curiosity and in stubborn patience.

At thirteen, Michael found work as an errand boy for George Riebau, a bookseller and bookbinder in London. His duties included carrying newspapers to the shop's customers and fetching them back again, since they were lent out as well as sold. He did the work so willingly and so carefully that his master soon had greater plans for him.

A year later, he was taken on as an apprentice, bound to Riebau for seven years to learn the craft of bookbinding. The work meant folding, stitching and pressing sheets of paper and covering them in leather, and it gave him quick and careful hands. It also placed him, almost by accident, among shelves of printed knowledge, which he could not resist reading.

Michael did not merely bind the books that passed through his hands; he read them, sometimes late into the evening. Two of them changed the direction of his life: an article on electricity in an encyclopaedia, and a clear little book called Conversations on Chemistry, written by Jane Marcet. They convinced him that nature could be understood by anyone patient enough to test it for himself.

Reading alone could not satisfy him, and he began to test what the books claimed. With a glass bottle and a few simple pieces of equipment, he built a small machine to make electricity and carried out his first experiments in his spare hours. It was a modest laboratory, but it was the beginning of a lifetime of discovery.

In 1812, a customer at the shop, William Dance, was so struck by the apprentice's enthusiasm that he gave him tickets to hear the great chemist Humphry Davy lecture at the Royal Institution. Michael took his place in the crowded hall and drank in all four of the lectures with delight. For a young man who had never seen a real laboratory, it must have felt like stepping into another world.

Michael wrote careful notes during each lecture and, once home, copied them out neatly with drawings of the apparatus. He bound the result into a handsome book of about three hundred pages and sent it to Davy, together with a request for any kind of work in science. It was a bold step for a bookbinder's apprentice, and it was the right one.

Davy was impressed by the book, and in March 1813, when a vacancy opened, he hired its author as his assistant at the Royal Institution. A few months later the two men set out on a long tour of Europe, where the young Faraday met many leading scientists. The boy who once carried newspapers had become a traveller and a student of the finest minds of his day.

In the years that followed, Faraday worked tirelessly at the Royal Institution and rose to become one of the foremost scientists of his age. In 1825 he began the Christmas Lectures for young people, a custom that has continued there ever since. When he stood before the children and lit his candle, he was speaking to an audience much like the boy he had once been.

He wanted his audience to see how many kinds of fuel a candle can be made from. Behind every one of them, he suggested, lay the same simple idea: a solid fuel, a wick and a flame.

Tallow, the rendered fat of cattle and sheep, made the cheapest candles of all. It melts easily, gives off a heavy and often unpleasant smell, and burns with a rather smoky flame. Even so, it lit ordinary homes, workshops and farms for many centuries, because almost anyone could afford it.

Beeswax is made by honeybees, who produce it in order to build the delicate walls of their honeycomb. Candles made from it were treasured because they burn slowly and cleanly, and give off a faint and pleasant scent of honey.
