Spermaceti is a pale and waxy substance taken from the head of the sperm whale, and it made some of the finest candles of the age. The candles were hard, bright and almost free of smell, and they burned with a calm and steady flame. They were also costly, which is why they were found in wealthy homes rather than in cottages.

In the 1820s, the French chemist Michel Chevreul took part in work that showed how the hard part of animal fat, known as stearin, could be separated from the soft part. Candles made from stearin were firmer, cleaner and far less smelly than the old tallow ones. It was a fine example of chemistry quietly improving the everyday lives of ordinary people in every town.

Many candles were made by hanging a row of wicks over a pot of hot melted fat and dipping them again and again. Each dip added a thin coat, and the candle slowly grew thicker until it was as wide as the maker wished. The patience that the craft demanded is easy to forget when we buy candles by the box.

Poor families sometimes made their own light from a rush, a thin dry plant stem that was peeled and dipped in fat. A rushlight gave only a weak and flickering glow and burned for a short time, but it cost next to nothing. Millions of evenings in humble homes were lit in this way, long before gas and electricity arrived.

At the heart of every candle lies a wick, usually made of twisted cotton threads that draw up the melted fuel. The wicks in old tallow candles tended to bend over and smoke, and so people trimmed them regularly with a pair of snuffers, which looked a little like scissors. A careless hand could easily put the flame out altogether, which is why the work needed some skill.

A plaited wick is woven in such a way that it curls over to one side as it burns. Its tip then reaches the outer edge of the flame, where the air is plentiful, and burns away without leaving a stump. Candles made with this clever wick, Faraday pointed out, never need to be trimmed at all.

In the days before cheap clocks, people sometimes marked a candle with a series of lines so that it could tell the time. As the wax burned down past each line, they knew that another hour had passed. The steadiness of a candle's burning, which Faraday was about to explain, made the idea possible.

When Faraday touched a lighted match to the wick, only a small blue flame appeared at first, hardly bigger than a pea. Over the next minute it grew steadily larger and brighter, as the heat gathered and more wax melted around it. He asked the audience to watch this slow awakening, for it was the first clue to how a candle works.

The heat of the flame melts the wax close to the wick, and the liquid gathers in a small, neat cup around it. Faraday invited his listeners to examine this cup closely, because its shape is no accident. It is the first piece of machinery in the whole contraption of the candle.

The rim of the cup stays solid, because the stream of air that rushes up toward the flame also cools the outer wall of the candle as it passes. The wax there is therefore kept firm, and it forms a wall that holds the melted fuel like a bowl. A candle, in other words, builds the very vessel that it needs, and then trusts the air to keep it whole.

In a draught, the air no longer flows evenly around the candle, and one side of the rim is cooled less than the rest. The wax on that side melts, spills over and runs down the outside of the candle in a thin stream, where it is wasted. The beauty of the cup, Faraday remarked, depends on the air being still and the flow being steady.

Seen in this way, a candle is simply a lamp that makes its own bowl, holding its own supply of liquid fuel. The solid wax turns to liquid in the cup, and the liquid, as we shall see, prepares itself to feed the flame. It is a more ingenious arrangement than most people suspect when they strike a match.

The liquid wax does not merely sit in the cup but climbs up the wick, against the pull of gravity, as though some invisible hand were drawing it upward. The explanation lies in the structure of the wick, which is made of many fine threads with minute spaces between them. The liquid creeps into those narrow channels and rises along them, which is why the flame never runs short of fuel.

Water behaves in just the same way when the corner of a sponge or a towel is dipped into a basin. It climbs up into the dry material, rising well above the level of the pool below, until the whole thing is damp. What happens in the wick is therefore not a special trick of candles but a very common property of liquids.

The narrower a glass tube, the higher the water will climb up inside it, and the finest tubes make it climb highest of all. Faraday called this action capillary attraction, a name taken from the Latin word for hair, because the narrowest tubes are about as fine as a single hair. The spaces between the threads of a wick are narrow enough to lift the liquid wax very effectively.

Anyone can watch the same action at breakfast by touching the corner of a sugar lump to the surface of a cup of tea. The tea steals upward through the tiny gaps in the sugar until the whole lump is soaked. It is a humble experiment, but it shows exactly how the fuel of a candle travels.

Only the tip of the wick actually burns, because the wax that keeps flowing up through it also keeps it from becoming too hot. A wick that is too thick brings up more fuel than the flame can consume, and the candle begins to smoke, while one that is too thin starves the flame. The candle-maker's art lies in finding the right balance between the two, and the wick is the key to it.

Faraday blew out the candle, and a thin white trail of smoke curled up from the black wick and wavered in the still air of the hall. He asked the children to keep their eyes on it, for it was about to teach them something that they could never have guessed. Even a dead candle, it seemed, still had a lesson to give to anyone who cared to look.

He took a lighted taper and held it in the white trail, a little way above the wick. The fire ran down the trail with a small flash and lit the wick again, as though the smoke were a fuse leading back to the candle. What he had shown, he explained, was that this white vapour was itself a fuel, and that it could burn.

Faraday now set out the long journey that the fuel makes inside a burning candle. The solid wax first melts into a liquid, the liquid climbs the wick and is turned by the heat into a vapour, and only then does the vapour burn. A flame, in other words, does not eat solid wax at all; it feeds on the gas that the wax gives off.

To prove that the flame is full of vapour, Faraday pushed one end of a thin glass tube into its dark middle, where there is no burning at all. White vapour travelled along the tube, much as smoke travels up a chimney, and came out at the far end. The dark centre of the flame, it seemed, was less an emptiness than a store of fuel waiting its turn.

He bent the tube so that its far end stood a little way from the candle, and he lit the vapour that came out of it. It burned at the end of the glass like a second small candle, while the first flame carried on burning as if nothing had happened. Few things in the lecture made the children gasp as loudly as this simple and beautiful trick.

Faraday pressed a piece of card flat across the flame for just a moment and then held it up for everyone to see. It was scorched brown in a ring, with a paler patch in the middle, which showed that the burning takes place in a thin shell around the outside. The flame, in short, is a hollow thing, and most of its inside is vapour that has not yet found any air.

Next Faraday held a piece of fine wire gauze, which looks something like a very close metal net, down over the candle flame. To the surprise of the audience, the flame could not pass through it, and the gauze held the fire back as firmly as a closed door. The flame rose to the gauze, flattened itself against the wire, and stopped, as if it had met a wall.

When Faraday lit the smoke that had risen above the gauze, it burned there as a separate flame, perched on top of the wire. The fire did not run down through the metal, and the candle beneath it was left in peace. The gauze, it appeared, would allow the vapour to pass but would never permit the fire to travel backward.

Humphry Davy, the very man who had once given Faraday his chance, used exactly this principle to make a safe lamp for coal miners in 1815. Before that time, the naked flame of a miner's candle could set fire to the explosive gas that sometimes seeps into a mine, with terrible results. Davy surrounded the flame with a cylinder of wire gauze, and the miners could work with far less fear.

The metal of the gauze carries the heat away so rapidly that the gas outside it cannot be made hot enough to catch fire, even though it may be seeping through the wire. Davy chose not to take out a patent on his lamp, so that any mine in the world might use it freely and without payment. It is a fine instance of an idea from the laboratory saving lives in the dark.

In still air, the flame of a candle is shaped like a tongue, tall and narrow, with a pointed tip that sways a little as though it were alive. Faraday told the audience that this familiar shape is not an accident of nature but a message about the air that surrounds the flame. To read the message, he said, they had only to ask what the flame does to the air.

The flame heats the air near it, and hot air, being lighter than cold, rises. Cooler air rushes in from below to take its place, and so a steady stream of air flows upward past the wick and stretches the flame into its long, pointed form. The tongue of fire is, in a sense, a picture of that invisible current.

To make the invisible stream visible, Faraday shone a strong lamp so that the shadow of the candle fell on a white screen. Above the flame, the rising hot air showed itself as a dark and wavering ribbon in the shadow, a column of something that nobody could normally see. A flame, it turned out, is also a kind of chimney, and the air that streams through it gives the flame its shape.

A gentle breath or a draught pushes the flame sideways, so that it flickers, leans and changes shape from moment to moment. Only in perfectly still air does a flame keep its calm and graceful tongue. Anyone who has tried to shield a candle on a windy evening has felt the truth of this.

In the 1780s, a Swiss scientist named Argand invented a lamp that gave a far better light than any candle could. Its wick was woven into a hollow ring instead of a flat strip, a change that looks small but turned out to matter a great deal. It was one of those inventions that seem obvious only after somebody has thought of them.

Air could reach the ring-shaped flame from two directions at once, from outside the ring and up through its hollow middle. With so much air, the fuel burned thoroughly and gave a bright, white and remarkably steady light. The old flame had been starved, and now at last it could breathe freely and burn as it was meant to burn.

Argand's burner was also fitted with a tall glass chimney, and this was the second part of his clever design. The hot air rises up the glass, which draws a strong and steady stream of fresh air in at the bottom and keeps the flame from wavering. Faraday lit one before his audience and let them admire how calmly it burned.

A chimney above a fire in a house works in precisely the same way. The hot air and smoke ascend it, drawn upward by their own lightness, and fresh air is pulled in through the room to feed the combustion. In this respect, the grandest hearth and the humblest lamp obey one and the same law.

Lamps of Argand's kind were far brighter than candles, and they spread quickly into homes, shops and lighthouses. Light for reading and for working, once a luxury, had become much easier to come by, and the evening hours were no longer wasted. It was a small revolution, and it had begun with nothing more than a ring-shaped wick and a glass tube.

With that, the first lecture came to its end, and the audience went home with plenty to think about. They had learned that the fuel of a candle melts, climbs the wick, turns into a vapour and burns, and that a current of fresh air feeds the flame from below. The next lecture would ask a new question: what makes that flame so bright?

In the second lecture, Faraday began by reminding the children of what they had learned the day before, and then he turned to a fresh puzzle. Why, he asked, does the flame of a candle shine so brightly, when so many other flames give hardly any light at all? The rest of the lecture was spent hunting for the answer, one experiment at a time.

He pointed out that not every flame gives a good light, and that some flames are dim to the point of being almost invisible. A spirit lamp, which burns alcohol, makes only a pale blue flame that lights a room hardly at all. Something in the candle's flame, it seemed, must be missing from the flame of the lamp, and Faraday meant to find out what.

Faraday suggested that a bright flame must contain something that shines, and he believed that it was solid matter in the form of tiny particles. Solid things glow when they are hot, he reminded his listeners, while gases, however hot, generally give out very little light. It was a bold guess, and he now set out to test it before their very eyes.

He held a thin platinum wire in the pale flame of the spirit lamp, and it glowed at once with a dazzling brightness. The wire was a solid, and the heat was making it shine, although the flame around it gave almost no light of its own. The point was plain to everyone in the hall, even to those who sat at the very back.

Next he sprinkled a pinch of fine iron filings into the flame, and the audience watched closely. Each tiny speck caught fire and burned with a bright spark, so that the flame suddenly became full of glittering, dancing light. Here, in miniature, was a flame that shone because it was crowded with burning solids.

Faraday then blew a little lycopodium powder through a flame, and the audience saw it burst into a great flash. This pale yellow powder, made from the spores of a plant, burns all at once in a vivid ball of fire, a little like a small bolt of lightning. It is a dangerous trick, and one that should be left to trained people.

Any solid thing will begin to glow if it is made hot enough, and the colour of its glow changes as the heat increases. A blacksmith like Faraday's father sees iron glow a dull red when it is warm, then orange, and finally almost white as it grows hotter still. The same law, Faraday said, was about to explain the candle, and a good deal else besides.

A glowing coal in a fire shows exactly the same thing, and it is a thing worth remembering. It may have no flame of its own, yet it shines a deep red, because it is a solid that has been made very hot. The radiance of the coal and the brilliance of the candle, he hinted, share a common origin.

So where do the solid pieces in a candle flame come from, and what makes them appear in the flame at all? Inside the flame, the great heat tears the wax vapour apart and sets free countless tiny particles of black carbon, each far too small to be seen on its own. Faraday had now found, in a single idea, the secret of the flame's brightness.

These tiny particles are heated until they glow white hot, and together they give the flame nearly all of its light. As they rise to the edge of the flame, they meet the air and burn away, and so a clean flame leaves no soot behind. The brilliant glow of a candle is, in the end, the light of burning carbon.

Faraday held a cold white saucer in the flame of the candle for just a moment. When he took it away and showed it to the audience, the underside was covered with a thick layer of black soot. The flame, it seemed, was carrying solid matter in its heart all the time.

This soot is carbon, the same black substance that is found in a lump of charcoal. Faraday added that even the sparkling diamond is made of carbon, one of the great surprises of chemistry, and a fact that must have startled many a listener. Two things could hardly be more unlike, and yet they were the same stuff.

Some materials make far more soot than a candle ever does, and they show the matter clearly. Camphor, a white and waxy solid that comes from a tree, burns with a thick and strongly smoking flame that sends up dark streamers into the air. It is a handsome illustration of what happens when a fuel carries more carbon than the flame can handle.

Turpentine, which is made from the sap of pine trees, behaves in much the same way. When Faraday set a little of it alight in a dish, great black clouds of smoke rolled up and drifted across the hall. The audience could see, at a glance, how different this flame was from the clean and quiet flame of a candle.

These flames smoke because they hold more carbon than the air can burn up at once. The carbon that is left over escapes unburned, in a cloud of tiny solid specks, and it floats away as black smoke or settles as soot on anything nearby. A smoky flame, then, is simply a flame that has been given too much fuel for the air at its disposal.

A candle burns without smoke because its flame meets just enough air to consume all the carbon that it sets free. The tiny black particles glow, then burn up completely at the edge of the flame, and nothing remains to drift away. It is a quiet and almost perfect piece of engineering, and it works without any help from us.

Anyone who has ever trimmed an oil lamp has met the same truth at first hand. When the wick is turned up too high, the flame suddenly begins to smoke, and a little black thread of soot climbs toward the ceiling, while turning the wick down again puts the matter right. The balance between fuel and air is the whole secret of a clean flame.

In Faraday's London, thousands of coal fires and chimneys filled the air with smoke, and the whole city lived with the consequences. Buildings were darkened with soot, washing hung out to dry came in grey, and on bad days a thick brown fog hung over the streets. The smoke of a single lamp was only a small sample of what the great city produced.

Soot, however, is not entirely a nuisance, and in fact it has its uses in the world of work. Fine black soot, known as lampblack, has long been collected and used to make black ink and paint, so that a by-product of the lamp helped to record the thoughts of people everywhere. Humble things, it seems, are seldom useless, and the lamp's own smoke is no exception to the rule.

Faraday ended this part of the lecture with a question for the children to take home. If a clean flame burns up all of its carbon, so that no soot is left and no smoke rises, he asked, where does that carbon go? It was the first of several mysteries that the candle would help them to solve.

Faraday placed a tall glass jar over a burning candle and asked the audience to watch the flame. It grew smaller and dimmer as the seconds passed, and after a short time it went out altogether, leaving only a thread of smoke. Something in the jar, it appeared, had been used up, and the flame had died for want of it.

The jar was still full of air, and yet the candle could no longer burn in it. Faraday explained that the air must have been changed by the burning, so that it had lost the power to keep a flame alive. Air that has done its work for one fire, in other words, cannot easily do it for another.

He then put two candles into two bottles, one open at the top and the other closed with a cork. The candle in the open bottle burned brightly and calmly, drawing in fresh air from the room, while the one in the closed bottle soon sank low and went out. A flame, he said, can no more live without fresh air than we can.

He lowered a burning candle on a wire into a tall glass jar and asked the children to watch what happened as it descended. At first it burned well, but as it went deeper the flame grew weaker and more feeble, until at last it could not burn at all. The lower air, it seemed, was already spoiled, and the flame could find no help in it at all.

A blacksmith, like Faraday's father, makes a fire hotter by blowing a stream of air through it with a pair of bellows. The more air the fire is given, the faster the fuel burns and the more brightly it glows, so that a few strong breaths can turn a dull red bed of coals into a dazzling heat. The smith knew all this long before the chemists could explain it, and his whole craft depended on it.

Faraday also made use of the Argand lamp to show how closely a flame depends on its air. When the stream of air that rises through the middle of the flame was shut off, the flame turned dull and yellow and began to give out thick smoke. When the air was let back in, it recovered its clear, white light at once.

A stove or a fire in a grate follows exactly the same rule as the candle in the jar. If its door and air vents are opened, it roars and burns fiercely, and if they are closed, it burns low and slowly, using its fuel at a gentle pace. The householder who regulates a fire is, without knowing it, doing a chemist's experiment.

A big jar lets a candle burn for longer than a small jar does, simply because it holds more air for the flame to use. This shows beyond doubt that a candle uses up something in the air as it burns, and that when the supply has gone, the flame must go with it. The same arithmetic, as we shall see, applies equally to a living person breathing in a shut room.

Yet the candle does not use up all of the air in the jar, and some of it remains when the flame has died. Faraday explained that only one part of the air keeps a flame alive, and that the rest, which makes up most of the jar, does nothing to help it. Which part was the useful one, he promised, would be revealed in a later lecture.

That was the end of the second lecture, and the children had learned a great deal about the secret life of a flame. Faraday told them that burning produces something new as well as consuming the air, and that on the next occasion they would discover what it was. The next lecture, he promised, would begin with a very ordinary object: a cold glass held over a flame.

At the start of the third lecture, Faraday asked a new question that followed from the last: what does a burning candle make? The air left in a jar after a flame has died is changed, he reminded his listeners, and he wanted to know what had been added to it. The answer, he promised, would be found in the plainest of places, and he would show it to them at once.

He held a shiny, cold cup over the flame of a candle and asked the children to watch the surface of the glass. Very soon the outside of the cup was clouded with tiny drops, which grew, ran together and trickled down in little streams. It looked exactly like the dew that gathers on a window on a cold morning.

To catch more of the drops, Faraday filled a metal vessel with a mixture of ice and salt, which is far colder than ice alone. He held the vessel over a flame, and the water gathered thickly on its chilly sides and dripped into a dish below. It was clear that the flame was giving up something to the cold metal.

The drops ran together into a small pool of clear liquid with no colour and no smell. It looked exactly like water, and Faraday declared that it was water, but he wanted to prove it beyond any shadow of doubt. A scientist, after all, is not satisfied until he has tested his claim, and Faraday was a scientist to the bone.

A warm cup, by contrast, stays quite dry when it is held over a flame, however long it is left there. The water is present all the same, but it remains in the air as an invisible vapour until something cold comes along and makes it gather into drops. The cold cup does not make the water; it merely reveals it to anyone who is watching closely.

Water is a marvellous substance, for it can be solid ice, flowing liquid or invisible steam, and yet it is the very same stuff in each of its three forms. Faraday showed all of them in turn, with a block of ice, a glass of water and a steaming kettle. The only real difference between them, he explained, is how hot they are, and how much heat they hold.

When water freezes it expands, and it can burst a bottle or a metal pipe if it has no room in which to grow. That is why water pipes so often split in the depths of a hard winter, and why a bottle left outside on a frosty night may be found in pieces by morning. The force of freezing water, though quiet, is very great, and no ordinary bottle can resist it.

Steam itself is a gas, and like most gases it cannot be seen at all, however hot it may be. The white cloud that rises above a kettle is made of tiny drops that have already cooled, which is why a clear gap can be seen between the spout and the cloud. What we call steam in everyday speech is really water in the act of returning to liquid.

Rain falls upon the hills and flows down the rivers to the sea, where it gathers in vast quantities. The sun then lifts water from the sea into the air again, clouds form, and the great cycle goes on without end. A candle, as Faraday would show, adds its own small share to the round.

Faraday told the children that a burning candle produces water too, a very little at a time, and that this water drifts into the air along with the other things it makes. Yet it was one thing to say so, and quite another to demonstrate that the drops had truly come from the flame and not merely from the surrounding air. For that he required something dramatic, and he had it waiting on the table.

Faraday took out a lump of potassium, a soft, silvery metal that has to be kept under oil because it reacts so readily with the air. It is so soft that it can be cut with a knife, and the fresh cut shines like silver for only a moment before it dulls. He handled it with great care, and so should anyone who ever meets it.

He dropped a small piece of the metal onto a dish of water, and the audience leaned forward. It skated across the surface, hissing and darting this way and that, and burst into a bright lilac flame. This, he said, is what potassium always does when it touches water, and it never fails to astonish the onlookers.

Then he dropped a piece into the drops he had caught from the candle, which looked just like ordinary water. The potassium behaved in exactly the same way, skating and burning with the same lilac flame, and that proved beyond argument that the liquid from the candle really was water. The candle, in burning, had made that water, just as surely as a kettle makes steam.

Potassium is not found as a metal anywhere in nature, and for a long time nobody had seen it at all. Humphry Davy first made it in 1807, by passing a strong electric current through potash, a substance obtained long ago from the ashes of plants. It was one of the great triumphs of Davy's career, and Faraday, who later worked beside him, knew it well.

The potassium takes something away from the water, and the gas that is set free is what burns. The lilac colour of the flame belongs to the potassium itself, but the fire is fed by a gas that the water has been forced to give up. In that moment, water was being taken to pieces before the eyes of the audience.

Faraday also heated a quantity of iron in a tube and passed steam over it. The iron took something from the steam and turned black and brittle, and a gas came out at the end of the tube that could be set alight and burned with a pale flame. Different metals, it appeared, can all pull the same gas out of water, and each does so in its own way.

A battery gives a steady flow of electricity, and the first practical one was made by Alessandro Volta in Italy in 1800. It was a tall pile of metal discs, separated by pieces of damp cloth, which gave a current for as long as the damp lasted. Without the battery, much of Faraday's later work on electricity and chemistry would have been quite impossible.

Faraday connected two wires from a battery to a dish of water, and tiny bubbles of gas began to rise from the end of each wire. He caught them in two glass tubes, one for each wire, so that the gases could be measured and tested separately. The water seemed to boil, though it was perfectly cold, and the children watched the bubbles with fascination.

One tube filled with exactly twice as much gas as the other, and the two gases proved to be quite different, for one of them burned and the other made things burn more fiercely. That told the children that water is not a simple substance at all but is made of two things joined together. The candle, they began to suspect, had been working on those two things all along.

Faraday went on to study the links between electricity and chemistry very closely, and he helped to invent words such as electrode and ion that scientists still use. It was a long way from the drops on a cold cup, but it began with the same simple question. What is water made of, and how does a flame come to make it?

In the fourth lecture, Faraday told the children that the water made by the candle must now be looked at more closely. Water, as the battery had shown them, is composed of two things, he reminded them, and the first of these is called hydrogen. It was now time, he said, to meet this remarkable substance face to face and to learn its habits.

To make hydrogen, Faraday put pieces of zinc in a bottle and added a weak acid. The metal fizzed busily, and a colourless gas bubbled out through a tube and was collected in a jar standing upside down in water. It is work for a trained chemist, and not something to try at home.

Hydrogen is the lightest gas of all, about fourteen times lighter than air, and it behaves like a bubble in a bath. Soap bubbles filled with it rise swiftly up to the ceiling, as Faraday showed, drifting upward until they burst. A gas that is lighter than air, he said, must go up as surely as a cork goes up in water.

Because hydrogen is so light, it was used in the very first balloons that ever carried people into the air. In December 1783, two men rose over Paris in a balloon filled with hydrogen, and they landed safely after about two hours in the air. A great crowd watched them climb into the sky above the city, and it must have seemed like a miracle.

Faraday held a jar of hydrogen with its mouth pointing down and pushed a lighted taper up into it. The hydrogen caught fire at the mouth of the jar and burned there with a quiet flame, but the taper went out as soon as it went further in. The gas, it was clear, could burn, but it could not help a candle to burn.

Hydrogen burns with a very pale flame, so pale that in a bright room it can hardly be seen at all, and it gives almost no light. This fits Faraday's idea exactly, because there are no solid particles in such a flame to glow. It was a fine example of an experiment agreeing with an explanation, which is exactly what scientists hope for.

When a cold, dry glass was held over the hydrogen flame, drops of water quickly formed on its surface and began to trickle down. Burning one kilogram of hydrogen makes nine kilograms of water, because oxygen from the air joins it in the burning. The only thing that this flame produces, in other words, is water, and nothing else at all.

Faraday held a fine platinum wire in the pale hydrogen flame, and it glowed with a brilliant white light. It was a second proof that a flame shines when it has solid matter in it, and not merely when it is hot, since the hydrogen flame is very hot indeed. The wire lit up the lecture hall as a candle never could, and the audience saw the lesson plainly.

The wax of a candle holds hydrogen as well as carbon, and the two are bound together in its molecules. When the wax burns, the carbon makes the light by glowing in the flame, and the hydrogen burns to make the very water that Faraday had collected on the cold cup. The mystery of the dew on the cold cup was solved at last, and the solution lay in the wax itself.

Hydrogen mixed with air burns almost all at once, with a sharp bang, and so it is dangerous in the wrong hands. A candle burns calmly because its fuel comes off the melted wax only a little at a time, and that patient pace is what makes it such a safe and faithful light. Faraday meant his young listeners to feel the difference, and to understand why the candle is such a safe teacher.

In the fifth lecture, Faraday turned at last to the other part of water, a gas that is called oxygen. Chemists had first made it in the 1770s, and it was soon found to be the part of the air that keeps a flame alive. It was, in a sense, the missing character in the story of the candle.

To make oxygen, Faraday heated a white powder called chlorate of potash together with a black powder called manganese dioxide in a glass flask. The black powder helps the white one to give up its oxygen more readily, and it is not used up in the process. It is a trick that chemists still admire for its neatness, and it works as well today as it did then.

A tube carried the gas from the flask into a jar full of water that stood upside down in a trough. The gas bubbled up into the jar, pushed the water out before it, and went on rising until the jar was filled with oxygen alone. Nothing could be seen inside it, for the gas, like air, is quite clear.

Oxygen has no colour, taste or smell, and it cannot be seen at all, so Faraday needed some way to prove that it was really there. He pushed a glowing splinter of wood into the jar, and it burst into flame at once, as though it had been touched by a spark. The audience saw the evidence with their own eyes, and Faraday invited them to see how simple the test was.

A candle lowered into a jar of oxygen burned far more brilliantly than it does in ordinary air. The flame grew larger and whiter, and it gave out a dazzling light that made the hall seem dim by comparison. This was the very gas, Faraday explained, that the candle had been seeking in the air all along.

Faraday then lowered a piece of red-hot charcoal into the oxygen, and the change was dramatic. It glowed fiercely and threw out bright sparks in every direction, though in the open air it had only glowed a dull and sullen red. The charcoal, like the candle, was feeding on oxygen, and it was feeding far faster than before.

A tiny piece of phosphorus, which only a trained chemist should handle, was lit and lowered into the jar. It burned with such a dazzling white light that the audience could hardly bear to look at it, and the jar was soon filled with a cloud of white smoke. Such is the fierce appetite of a flame for oxygen, Faraday said, when oxygen is plentiful.

Sulphur burns with a small and rather timid blue flame in the open air. In a jar of oxygen, the very same sulphur burns with a splendid violet flame and gives off a sharp and choking smell, which is a good reason for leaving such experiments to experts. The difference is simply the richer supply of oxygen, which lets the sulphur burn faster and hotter.

A thin iron wire, which can hardly be made to burn in air, burns well in a jar of oxygen. When one end had been heated and lowered into the jar, the wire kindled with a fierce light and sent out a shower of glittering sparks, which fell like tiny stars. It was a striking proof of the power of the gas, and it was made with the simplest of materials.

Oxygen is found almost everywhere on Earth, and we meet it every minute of our lives. It is in the air that we breathe and in the water that we drink, and it makes up nearly half the weight of the rocks of the Earth's crust. Faraday had set out to explain a candle, and he had found one of the commonest substances in the world.

The air around us is not one gas but a mixture of several gases, mingled so thoroughly that we never notice the fact. About one fifth of it is oxygen, and Faraday explained that this is the part that keeps a flame alive. The remaining four fifths, he said, have a very different character, and they do very little to help a fire.

Chemists can show how much oxygen the air holds by burning something in a closed jar that stands over water, and then watching what happens when the flame dies. The burning uses up the oxygen, and the water rises in the jar to fill about one fifth of its volume. The empty space marks exactly the share that the fire has taken, and no more than that.

The rest of the air is mostly a gas called nitrogen, which is quiet, colourless and curiously inactive. A lighted match plunged into pure nitrogen goes out at once, because nitrogen does not burn and does not help other things to burn. It is as though the gas simply declines to take part in the fire.

Nitrogen may seem a useless gas, but in fact it has an important task to perform. It spreads the oxygen out, so that things burn steadily in air and not fiercely, as they do in pure oxygen. Without it, every fire would leap up like the candle in the jar of oxygen, and the world would be a far more dangerous place.

The two main gases in the air are only mixed together, not joined, and that is an important difference. Because they are merely mingled, they can be separated again, and today a great deal of oxygen is taken from the air for use in hospitals and in industry. A true chemical compound could not be taken apart so easily, and that is how chemists tell the two apart.

Air may seem to be nothing at all, yet it has weight, and a good deal of it. A litre of air weighs a little more than a gram, so that a big room full of it weighs about as much as a grown person. Faraday asked his listeners to remember this the next time they thought the room was empty.

Because air has weight, the whole depth of the sky presses down on everything beneath it, and the pressure is far greater than most people suppose. At sea level it is about the weight of a kilogram on every square centimetre of surface, which means that even the palm of a hand carries a substantial load. We are simply so used to the load that we never notice it, and it never seems heavy at all.

Faraday showed the strength of this pressure with an air pump and a tall glass jar, and the demonstration made the audience gasp. When the air had been pumped out of the jar, the hand that covered its open end was pressed down firmly by the weight of the air above, and it could not easily be lifted. The invisible sea of air, it seemed, could grip as tightly as a vice.

We do not feel the air pressing on us, because the air inside our bodies pushes back with equal force, and the two pressures balance one another. It is only when the balance is upset that we notice it, as our ears do when we drive up a steep hill or ride quickly in a fast lift. The sensation is a small reminder of an ever-present pressure, and it passes as soon as the balance returns.

The air stretches upward for many miles above our heads, growing thinner and thinner as it rises. On a high mountain there is so little air that climbers must breathe harder, and the very highest peaks are hard to climb without extra oxygen. Our whole world, Faraday suggested, lies at the bottom of a deep ocean of gas.

A candle burns away, and the wax seems to vanish into nothing, as though it had been spirited out of the world. Faraday told the children that nothing is really lost, because every part of it turns into invisible gases that mix quietly with the air. The candle has not truly disappeared, because it has only changed its shape, and every part of it is still somewhere in the air around the table.

Faraday held a jar over the flame for a while, so that it filled with the gases that rose from it, and then he added some clear limewater and shook it. The limewater turned milky white at once, which showed that the candle had made a second gas, quite different from the water that he had caught before. The new gas was an invisible thing, and yet it had left a plain and visible mark on the liquid for everyone in the room to see.

Limewater is made by stirring a little lime into water and letting the mixture settle until the liquid above it is quite clear. Lime itself is made by heating chalk or limestone in a very hot fire, a craft that is thousands of years old. It is a plain and cheap liquid, but to a chemist it is a very sensitive test.

To collect more of the gas, Faraday drew the air from above a burning candle through a tube into a bottle of limewater, so that the products of the flame were forced to pass through the liquid. It bubbled up through the clear fluid, and the limewater slowly turned the colour of milk. The candle was clearly making something that the eye could not see, and it was making it all the time that the flame burned quietly on the table.

Faraday then burned a piece of charcoal in a jar of oxygen, which made it glow and spark fiercely, and when the burning was over he shook the jar with limewater. The limewater turned milky in exactly the same way, and the audience could see that the two gases were the same. Whatever the candle made as it burned, the charcoal made too, and the plain black lump had suddenly become part of the same story as the flame.

Charcoal is almost pure carbon, so the milky limewater showed that the gas comes from carbon joining with oxygen from the air. The candle, which holds a great deal of carbon in its wax, makes the very same gas as it burns, and the black soot of the smoky flame had been a clue all along. The carbon had not vanished from the smoke at all, because when the flame burned cleanly it had simply gone invisible, joined to the oxygen of the air.

In Faraday's day the gas was called carbonic acid, but we now call it carbon dioxide, which tells us more about what it is. The name means that every tiny piece of it has one atom of carbon joined to two atoms of oxygen, and so the gas is heavier than the carbon that went into it. It is a tidy name for a rather untidy discovery, one that took many chemists many years of patient and sometimes quarrelsome work to reach.

When the candle burns, the oxygen from the air joins with its carbon and its hydrogen, and the two new substances, water and carbon dioxide, go off into the room. That is why the gases that a candle makes would weigh more than the candle itself, if we could catch and weigh them all, because the oxygen has been added to them. The weight of the candle has not been destroyed; it has merely been joined by something from the air.

In chemistry, nothing is ever truly lost when something burns, although it may change its form so completely that nobody would recognise it. If a candle were burned inside a sealed jar that was weighed before and after, the weight would be exactly the same, because nothing could escape and nothing could enter. This simple rule governs every fire in the world, from a match to a forest.

The French chemist Antoine Lavoisier worked this out in the 1770s and 1780s, by weighing things before and after they burned with extraordinary care. He showed that burning is the joining of a fuel with oxygen from the air, and that nothing is lost in the process, only changed. His careful balance did more to tame the mystery of fire than a thousand years of guessing.

Faraday lowered a burning candle on a wire into a tall jar that looked quite empty, although it was full of carbon dioxide. The flame shrank, flickered and died almost at once, as though a hand had pinched it out. The gas that a flame itself makes cannot help any other flame to live.

Faraday explained to the children that carbon dioxide is a good deal heavier than air, and he showed them the difference with a balance. A jar of the gas weighs about one and a half times as much as a jar of ordinary air. Heaviness is a surprising quality to find in something that nobody can see, and it was soon to prove very useful.

Because the gas is so heavy, it can be poured like water, although the audience could not see a drop of it fall. Faraday tipped one jar over another, and then he held a candle in the lower jar, where the flame gave a last flicker and vanished. A murmur of delight ran round the room as the invisible stream proved itself.

Faraday laid a long wooden trough on the table and set a row of small candles along its bottom, each one burning cheerfully in the still air. When he poured the invisible gas into the upper end, the gas ran down the channel like a stream and the flames went out one after another. It was a neat and almost theatrical way to show that a gas can flow.

Next he dropped some lumps of white marble into a glass vessel of weak acid, and at once the stone began to fizz and bubble as though it were alive. The gas that rose from it was collected in jars and tested with a candle and with limewater, and it behaved in every way like the gas of the flame. Hard stone, it turns out, can hold the very gas that a candle breathes out.

Lime is made in great kilns, where the heat of a fierce fire drives the carbon dioxide out of limestone and leaves a white, crumbling solid called quicklime. It is from this quicklime that the limewater of the earlier experiments is made, so the test and the gas are bound together in a single circle. Stone, fire and flame all belong to one chemical family, and the candle on the table is only its smallest and most familiar member.

Chalk, marble and many seashells are made of the same substance, and a large part of it is carbon dioxide held tightly in a solid form. The white cliffs of southern England and the polished marble of a palace floor are, in this sense, hardened gas. Faraday liked to remind his listeners that great things are built of humble parts.

Carbon dioxide also dissolves in water, especially when it is squeezed into it under pressure, and Faraday pointed to a bottle of soda water as a familiar example. When the top is taken off, the pressure is released and the gas escapes in a stream of sparkling bubbles. The fizz that children enjoy at a party is the same gas that a candle makes as it burns.

Because it is heavy, the gas sinks and gathers in low places, such as old wells and the great vats where brewers ferment their beer. A person who climbs down into such a place can be in serious danger, since no one can breathe carbon dioxide and live, and a lantern lowered on a rope will warn of it by going out. It was a lesson that miners and well-diggers had learned long before any chemist explained it.

The same gas that a candle makes can therefore be used to put out a fire, and a good many modern fire extinguishers are filled with it for exactly this reason. It smothers a flame by pushing away the air that the fire needs, rather than by drowning it as water does. In a sense, a fire is ended by the very gas that its own burning has made, so that a flame can be said to carry the seeds of its own ending.

Faraday showed the children a lump of charcoal burning with a deep red glow and hardly any flame, unlike the bright tongue of the candle. Charcoal does not melt or turn into a vapour when it is heated, so there is no vapour above it for a flame to feed on. The burning goes on at the surface of the solid, quietly and steadily, like a coal in a grate.

Charcoal is made by heating wood with very little air, so that the carbon is left behind and most of the rest is driven away. Charcoal burners used to build a great mound of logs, cover it with turf and earth, and let it smoulder slowly for many days. The result was a light, black, brittle fuel that burned hotter and cleaner than wood.

When wood is heated without air, it gives off a thick and smoky vapour, and this vapour can be lit like the vapour of a candle. What remains in the pot afterwards is black and brittle, and it is nearly pure carbon, the same substance that glows in a flame and shows itself in soot. Fire, in other words, is a kind of sorting, in which some parts rise and some stay behind.

Faraday packed some small pieces of coal into the bowl of a clay pipe, sealed it with clay and set it in the heart of a fire. After a short while, a thin stream of gas came out of the stem of the pipe, and when he lit it with a taper, it burned with a bright and steady flame. The audience had seen a small gasworks at work, and the gas was very like the vapour of a candle.

In a gasworks, coal is heated in great closed ovens, and the gas that it gives off is collected, cleaned and led away through iron pipes. These pipes ran under the streets of the town to every house and lamp that was connected to them, like the roots of some enormous tree. A single set of ovens could thus light a whole district of the city for an evening, and no one needed to carry a flame from room to room.

What remains in the ovens after the gas has gone is coke, a hard, grey fuel that burns with very little smoke and is good for heating and for smelting iron. The gasworks also gives a thick black tar, which was at first a troublesome waste but later became the raw material for dyes, medicines and many other useful things. In this way, even the leavings of a lamp could be turned into a trade.

In the early years of the 1800s, London began to light its streets with coal gas, and the idea soon spread to other cities of Britain and Europe. Lamplighters went from post to post at dusk with their long poles, and the dark and dangerous streets became brighter and safer than they had ever been before. The people of the time marvelled that light could be brought through a pipe.

A gas jet looks very different from a candle, but it shines for the same reason, and Faraday took care to point this out to his listeners. Tiny pieces of carbon are set free in the flame, and they glow white hot before they burn away to carbon dioxide at the outer edge. The street lamp, the gas jet and the candle on the table are all one kind of lamp, burning different fuels.

Later, a burner designed by the German chemist Robert Bunsen mixed air with the gas before it was lit, and the effect was striking. The flame became hot and blue and gave hardly any light, because the carbon burned at once instead of glowing in the flame for a moment. It was a useful flame for laboratories, because it heated things without covering them in soot.

Coal itself is made from plants that grew in great forests many millions of years ago, long before any person walked the earth. As the dead trees and ferns were buried and pressed under later layers of earth, they slowly turned into the black rock that we dig up and burn today. A lump of coal is therefore stored sunlight, and when it burns, the old forest gives back its carbon to the air.

Faraday took a glass tube, put one end into a jar of clear limewater and breathed gently through the other. The limewater, which had stayed bright and still, turned milky white before the eyes of the children, in exactly the same way as it had for the gas from the candle. The audience could see that their own breath held the very substance of the flame.

A person's breath carries water as well as carbon dioxide, and anyone can see this by breathing on a cold window or a glass on a winter morning. The surface clouds over with a fine mist of tiny drops, just as the cold cup did when Faraday held it above the candle. The two experiments, which seemed so different at first, were plainly one and the same.

The air that we breathe out is quite different from the air that we breathe in, and Faraday used two jars to prove it. It has less oxygen in it, so that a candle burns poorly in it, and it holds far more carbon dioxide than the fresh air does. Every breath, in other words, is a small act of burning, and the air is changed by it.

Air travels down into the lungs, where it comes very close to the blood through walls so thin that they are almost not there at all. The blood takes up oxygen and carries it to every corner of the body, and on its return journey it brings back carbon dioxide to be breathed out into the room. A person is, in this sense, a kind of living furnace with a most elaborate set of pipes.

Sugar is made of carbon, hydrogen and oxygen, and Faraday showed what happens when a lump of it is heated in a spoon over a flame. It melts, bubbles and turns brown and then black, which shows that the carbon was hidden inside it, though a lump of sugar looks as white and pure as snow. In a human body, sugar is not blackened but burned slowly and gently, which is a far better use for it.

Faraday told his listeners that the food we eat is the fuel of the body, and that bread, fruit and meat are, in a way, the candles by which we live. Their carbon joins slowly with the oxygen that we breathe in, and the carbon dioxide that is made is carried away in the breath. The chemistry is the same as in the candle's flame, only a great deal more gentle.

This quiet burning inside the body gives out heat, which is why a healthy person stays warm even on a bitter winter day, long after a hot drink has gone cold. The normal temperature of the body is about 37 degrees Celsius, and it stays remarkably steady in a warm room or a cold one. No stove or lamp holds its heat so faithfully as the burning inside us.

When a person runs or works hard, the body needs more energy, and so the breathing becomes faster and deeper to bring in more oxygen. That is also why people who do hard physical work, or children who are growing quickly, need more food than those who sit still all day. The fire inside us, like any other, burns faster when it is given more air and more fuel.

In a shut room full of people, the air slowly changes as everyone breathes it in and out again, and it grows heavy and stale. It has a little less oxygen and a little more carbon dioxide than before, and the people in it soon feel tired and dull, which is why a teacher or a nurse opens a window. A candle, which is much more sensitive than a person, would show the change sooner still.

Faraday told the children that the burning of a candle and the breathing of a living creature are really one and the same thing. The candle burns brightly in the open air, while breathing goes on quietly and invisibly inside us, but in both cases carbon is joined to oxygen and carbon dioxide is made. The audience, which had come to see one small flame, left knowing that they carried a flame of their own.

Every fire, every lamp and every living creature on Earth sends carbon dioxide into the air, and they have done so for ages, in numbers too great to count. Faraday asked the children why the air does not become thick and poisonous with it, and the answer, he said, lay with the quiet, green things growing outside. It is a question that rarely occurs to us as we breathe, although the whole of life depends upon its answer.

Plants take carbon dioxide from the air through their leaves, and they build its carbon into their own stems, leaves, roots and fruit, so that the gas of the candle becomes part of a living body. The plant is, in a very real sense, made out of the air that the flames and the breath have sent into it. The farmer's fields and the forests beyond them are, in effect, great gardens of carbon, drawn out of the air by the light of the sun.

In 1771 the English chemist Joseph Priestley placed a sprig of mint in a jar of air that had been spoiled by a burning candle, so that no flame could live in it any longer. After some days he found that the air had become good again, and a candle could be lit in it once more. It was a simple experiment, but it opened the way to understanding how all of the living world is joined to the air.

Some years later, the Dutch doctor Jan Ingenhousz repeated the work and found that plants can only do this when sunlight falls on them. His experiments showed that the green leaves are doing important work, and that the light is needed to power it, just as a candle needs oxygen to burn. The sun, which seems so far away, turns out to be the engine of the whole business.

In bright sunlight a green leaf takes in carbon dioxide and gives out oxygen, and tiny bubbles can be seen rising from the leaves of a water plant held up to the window. In the dark the leaf stops making oxygen, which is why a plant needs the light and cannot thrive in a cupboard. Day after day, the green world quietly mends the damage done by every flame and every breath.

The wax, oil and fat of which candles are made come from plants, or from animals that have fed on plants, so that the candle on Faraday's table was itself once part of a living thing. Beeswax comes from bees that gather their food from flowers, and tallow comes from cattle that have eaten grass. The sunlight that fell on those fields has, in a sense, been waiting in the wax all this time.

A tall tree grows mostly from the air and from water, and only a small part of its substance comes from the soil beneath it. When a log burns on the hearth, the carbon that it gives back to the air is the carbon that the tree once took from it, and the warmth of the fire is the sunshine of many summers. It is a wonderful thing that a mighty oak can be built from something as thin as air.

Anyone can see the same balance in a bowl that holds a few fish and some green water plants standing in the light. The fish breathe out carbon dioxide, which the plants take in and use, and the plants give back the oxygen that the fish need, so that the two live together in a small, quiet bargain. The water in a good aquarium may stay fresh for a very long time, because its creatures are looking after one another.

So the carbon travels in a magnificent circle, passing from the air into the plants, and thence into the creatures that devour them, or into a flame, and so back to the atmosphere. It is never consumed and never squandered, but merely handed on from one body to another, and a candle's flame is a single small turn of that wheel. This is the thought that lends the whole course of lectures its profound and quiet unity.

The carbon dioxide of a single breath may one day become part of a leaf, and the leaf in turn may become food for some passing animal. A breath, which we scarcely notice, thus turns out to be a small portion of the vast circle of life, which has been turning for countless ages. Every child in that lecture hall belonged to that circle, as surely as the trees outside the building.

Faraday told the children that the same laws govern a candle, a plant and a person, and that no part of nature stands alone. Everything that burns, breathes or grows belongs to one connected whole, and a single flame can lead us a long way towards understanding it. The great is hidden in the small, and the lecture hall, with its one flame and its crowd of listening children, was the proof.

Burning, breathing and growing all turn out to be the same few substances changing partners, in a dance that never ends. Carbon, hydrogen and oxygen join and part and join again, and as they do so they pass through candles, plants and people, and through the air that lies between them. The enormous variety of the world rests upon a surprisingly small number of elements, which is perhaps the finest lesson of all.

Faraday urged the children to look at everything with care and to question whatever they saw, however plain it might seem. They were to trust only what they had tested for themselves, he said, even when a famous person told them otherwise. It is advice that every scientist, young or old, has good reason to remember, and it is as sound today as it was then.

Many of the experiments in the lectures are simple enough to be repeated at home with a candle, a plate, a glass jar and a little patience. A few of them, such as those with acids, hot metals and gases, belong in a laboratory, and a grown-up must always stand close by when fire is used. Curiosity is a fine thing, but it does best when it is also careful, patient and ready to ask for help.

Faraday said that the candle had taught only the first small lessons about nature, and that a great deal more remained for the children to learn. He did not pretend to have reached the end of the subject, and he hoped that someone in his audience might one day go further than he had. Honest modesty of this kind was always a part of his greatness, and it made his lectures all the more convincing to the young.

At the close of the last lecture, Faraday said that he hoped the children would be like candles, shining as lights to all those around them. He wished that in everything they did they might justify the beauty of the flame by doing their duty honestly and well, for the good of other people. It was a gentle and moving end to six evenings of fire and wonder, and it has been quoted by readers ever since.

By the end of the six lectures, one small flame had led the children through fire, water, air, carbon and breath, and through a good part of the chemistry of the world. Nothing grand had been needed to achieve it, only a long table, some pieces of glass and a candle that anyone might buy for a few pence. Faraday had demonstrated that a magnificent subject may begin with the humblest object in the house.

The lectures were printed as a book in 1861, from notes that the young chemist William Crookes took while Faraday spoke,, with Faraday's agreement. The volume has been translated into many languages and read across the globe ever since, and it is still regarded as one of the most admirable introductions to science ever composed. A candle, it seems, can go on shining long after the wax has gone, simply because its story was written down.

Faraday also made great discoveries about electricity and magnetism, and in 1831 he found the principle behind the electric generator and the motor. A unit of electrical measurement, the farad, is named after him, and his ideas lie behind almost every machine that is powered by electricity today. The boy who had bound other people's books became one of the most important scientists in history.

Next time you light a candle, you can see what Faraday saw: the little cup of wax, the climbing wick, the rising vapour, the glow of white-hot carbon and the unseen gases drifting away. You will know that the same laws govern the flame, the leaf and your own breath, and that they were worked out by looking closely at a plain thing. The smallest everyday things can lead to the biggest ideas, if only we look carefully enough.
